#4901. This Specific Type of ‘Bathing’ May Have Unexpected Immune Benefits

It’s gotten especially popular in the past few years.

Sitting in a sauna is a nice way to unwind, whether you're starting your day or coming down post-workout. But while it can feel good to lounge in the heat to decompress, research suggests you might be doing your immune system a solid in the process, too.

The study, which was published in the journal Temperature, found that hanging (or ‘bathing,’ as it’s called) in the sauna for 30 minutes sparks a unique chain reaction in the body that could support your health. Scientists haven't quite figured out what these changes mean when it comes to measurable impact on immunity, but doctors say this is definitely one more thing to mull over while you're getting your sauna on. Here's why.

Meet the experts: Jari Laukkanen, MD, PhD, study co-author and professor at the University of Eastern Finland; Eric Ascher, DO, family medicine physician at Northwell’s Lenox Hill Hospital; and Joseph J. Ciotola, MD, an orthopedic surgeon at Baltimore's Mercy Medical Center

For the study, researchers recruited 51 adults with an average age of 50. Scientists took blood samples before asking participants to sit in a 163-degree sauna for 30 minutes. The participants gave blood samples again right after the sauna session and again 30 minutes later.

The researchers found that there was a temporary increase in every type of circulating white blood cell they measured, including immune cells called neutrophils and lymphocytes. Neutrophils are usually the first defenders to respond to an infection and lymphocytes recognize specific threats, make antibodies, and help coordinate immune responses. The increase only lasted for 30 minutes—the neutrophil and lymphocyte counts returned to baseline after that.

"We have studied sauna bathing and cardiovascular health for many years, and our previous studies have shown interesting associations with better health outcomes," says Jari Laukkanen, MD, PhD, study co-author and professor at the University of Eastern Finland. "We wanted to understand more about the biological mechanisms behind these findings, including possible effects on the immune system."

Again, the researchers simply found that this jump in certain white blood cells happens when someone sits in a sauna—they didn't figure out why it happens or what it means. Still, experts have a few theories.

One is that sauna bathing presents a sudden physical challenge for the body, according to Eric Ascher, DO, a family medicine physician at Northwell’s Lenox Hill Hospital. "This heat stress wakes up your nervous system, causing white blood cells stored in different parts of your body to rush into your bloodstream," he says.

This is similar to what happens in the body when you do a cold plunge, says Joseph J. Ciotola, MD, an orthopedic surgeon at Baltimore's Mercy Medical Center. “It’s just hormetic stress,” he adds, referring to the process where short stressors can trigger a positive adaptive response in the body and make you stronger.

The release of these immune cells is also similar to what happens during physical exercise, Laukkanen says.

As for what this means for the body, that's still being explored. "White blood cells are important for immune defense and surveillance," Laukkanen says. "Their temporary mobilization may help the body respond to physiological challenges."

But Laukkanen also says that it's not clear yet what this means for immune health. "Our study measured acute responses after one sauna session, and we cannot yet say whether these changes improve long-term immunity or reduce the risk of infections," he says. "More research is needed."

You do more than just sweat in a sauna. "Saunas make your heart beat faster, and your blood vessels open up, which is very similar to the benefits you get from taking a brisk walk or going for a light run," Ascher says. "Because of this, regular sauna use has been linked to lower blood pressure, a healthier heart, and a lower risk of getting certain long-term diseases." (Still, he stresses that there's no data now to suggest that sauna use will replace the need for medication or exercise.)

Sauna use can also help people relax, recover from stress, and support overall well-being, Laukkanen says. "Sauna can be a pleasant part of a healthy lifestyle, alongside regular physical activity," he adds.

Of course, not everyone should hop in the sauna. "Because the intense heat puts a lot of stress on your heart and body, anyone with serious heart problems, very low blood pressure, or severe dizziness should stay out of saunas," Ascher says. Pregnant women and older adults may also want to steer clear.

But if you already like hanging in the sauna, it's nice to know you might be doing your immune system a solid while you kick back and enjoy.

#4899. 8 Best Hotel Mattress Picks for a Five-Star Staycation (2026)

The hotel mattress probably isn't on your vacation itinerary, but it can make or break the trip. A lumpy, unsupportive bed can derail even the most carefully planned getaway. A really good one, though, might become an unexpected highlight—the kind that has you looking forward to bedtime and quietly checking the mattress label before checkout.

Recreating that experience at home doesn't require another plane ticket. Some of our favorite properties, including design-forward waterfront retreats and charming bed-and-breakfasts, put just as much thought into their mattresses as they do their interiors. Many turn to brands like Saatva, Ostermoor, and Casper to outfit their guest rooms; others, like the W Hotels, have signature mattresses you can purchase directly. We've rounded up our favorites, such as options with plush pillow tops, supportive coils, and pressure-relieving foam, to help you bring home the best part of your stay. The room service, unfortunately, is still up to you.

For consistency, all the prices reflect queen-size mattresses.

A stay at the Ritz-Carlton is typically reflected by its refined, elegant bedrooms. The property’s eponymous bed invites the same feeling. At 14 inches, it’s a higher-profile mattress that can help make the bed the centerpiece of the room. One of the standout qualities is its coil system, as it includes 900-plus individual springs for great edge support to help keep the sides from sagging as well as promote motion isolation—a necessary factor for couples who don’t want to sense each other’s every move.

Serta is one of the most well-known mattress manufacturers for high-end hotels, such as the Waldorf-Astoria. While many luxury properties feature custom beds from the namesake brand, it doesn’t mean you can’t shop at popular retailers such as Amazon. You’d never guess it, but this premium bed is priced under $500 (making it the most affordable on our list). While Serta offers memory foam and hybrid versions of its beds, this pillow-top innerspring mattress has been a favorite in our shopping writer Julia Harrison’s space, and she says it lives up to its “Five-Star” name.

It’s filled with three zones of coil support that keep her free of back and neck problems, and the quilted cover gives her something soft to dream about each night. “I’m really not one for pomp and frills in my mattress—I’m a firm believer that a good mattress has very little going on besides a somewhat plush top to keep you from feeling any sort of spring mechanism going on inside,” she says in her mattress review. “I instantly slept well on this mattress I think because it’s quite simply: a great mattress.” Bonus: It’s a mattress-in-a-box, so it can fit easily through narrow doors and hallways once it’s delivered, and inflate to its full size in less than a day’s time after unboxing, according to Harrison. Just in case you’re on the fence, it comes with a 100-day sleep trial so you can really see if it’s right for you before committing.

The Six Bells Countryside Inn opened its doors in the bucolic Hudson Valley in 2025, and it’s already earned two Michelin Keys. In each of the 11 carefully and whimsically designed bedrooms at this retreat, you’ll find handcrafted mattresses and bedding from New York-born brand Ostermoor. Dating back to 1853, Ostermoor’s mattresses have a storied history. The beds have innovated to foam and pocketed coil inner layers and designer covers in recent years, and we can prove they’re worth the splurge.

“From the moment I plopped down on the mattress, I was amazed by how comfortable and supportive it was,” shares contributor Zoë Sessums. “It strikes a perfect balance between spring and cushion—just the right amount of give without ever feeling too soft. I consistently wake up feeling rested and supported.” Firm without feeling rigid, this mattress looks as good as it feels, too. “The tufted top, the blue and white ticking pattern, the hand-stitched details—it feels like a piece of luxury furniture, not just a place to sleep,” Sessums adds, later writing, “I would recommend this to someone who values design and craftsmanship as much as comfort.”

Saatva has found its way into charming bed-and-breakfasts and boutique retreats across the country, including Pasadena's historic Bissell House (an 1887 Victorian filled with antique furnishings) and the Cornell Inn in the Berkshires (known for its colorful, individually designed guest rooms). You can bring that same inviting comfort home with the Saatva Classic, which comes with a plush three-inch Euro pillow top, a responsive dual-coil system, and targeted lumbar support. “It’s firm (which I prefer), regulates temperature well, and is extremely durable,” our tester Erin Kaplan, vice president of communications at Conde Nast, says. “I alternate between sleeping on my side and sleeping on my stomach, and this mattress is great for both positions.”

Choose from three firmness levels—plush soft, luxury firm, or firm—, eight different sizes, and two mattress heights to find your ideal fit. Feeling extra? Saatva also offers two adjustable bases that elevate your head and feet at the touch of a button, including a premium Plus model for an even more indulgent breakfast in bed. A 365-night trial gives you plenty of time to sleep on your decision before committing.

At 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge, even the beds have a view. Sweeping views of the Manhattan skyline set the scene, with reclaimed wood floors, rich leather headboards, and locally crafted details like crate-inspired closets and Fresnel glass light fixtures bringing warmth and character to the rooms. With custom Keetsa mattresses in every room, you might find yourself hitting snooze despite the spectacular view.

Back at home, the Keetsa Pillow Plus offers its own take on hotel-worthy comfort. It's something of a Goldilocks mattress: not too soft, not too firm, but just right. A three-inch pillow top combines body-contouring memory foam with responsive comfort foam to help cushion pressure points, and a soft, moisture-wicking cover designed to keep overheating at bay. Individually wrapped coils provide cushioning and support while minimizing motion transfer, so even if your bedmate tosses and turns, you can stay blissfully unaware.

When husband-and-wife duo Ely and Danielle Franko transformed a dated Catskills ski hostel into The Henson, a 16-room boutique hotel, they had a pretty good idea of what makes a great night's sleep. The couple painstakingly restored the property themselves, filling its rooms with vintage furniture, locally sourced finds, and hand-applied wallpaper. But when it came to mattresses, they didn't have to look far for inspiration: They chose the same Casper Dream Hybrid they sleep on at home. In fact, they loved it so much that they insisted on king-size mattresses in every room, even the smallest ones. The hybrid design combines responsive springs with breathable foam and three zones of support that help keep your spine aligned. Its medium feel is meant to offer a little give without leaving you sinking into the mattress, making it a crowd-pleasing choice for your own guest room. After all, the best hosts know a good night's sleep is part of the hospitality.

Hot sleepers, here’s a mattress for you. The Four Season’s signature mattress features a couple of core cooling bed qualities: proprietary cooling gel foam layers with channeled designs that promote airflow throughout the mattress, as well as a patented DualCool top layer that draws heat and moisture away from the body and keeps the bed fresh with its antimicrobial properties. The cooling mattress is designed for sleepers who need extra structure on their bed. This posh number has targeted support for the lower back area and zeroes in on alignment regardless of your sleep style.

The W Hotels are widely popular because of the bold design across the properties worldwide. To mirror this aesthetic, you can cover the brand’s mattress with colorful bedding to let your personal style shine. When it comes to the bed itself, it is defined by a plush top quilted damask design to ease side sleepers into a peaceful slumber. It’s made for people who need extra support too, though, including an individually-wrapped coil system, five-zone support system, and comfort layers for added cushioning and pressure relief.

Which Kind of Mattress Do Five-Star Hotels Use?

Most luxury hotels use hybrid mattresses in their suites to strike the right balance of softness and support, thanks to pocketed coils and layers of foam. These are also typically medium-firm mattresses since a plush mattress can be uncomfortable for some sleep positions like stomach sleepers. Ultra-firm beds are often too stiff for side sleeping and may not align with guests' expectations who are looking for soft mattresses to sink into on their vacations.

If you want to refresh your mattress without the hefty price tag of buying a new one, a mattress topper or featherbed could be a solid transitional pick. The Ritz-Carlton and W Hotels promote one made with white duck feathers, Mandarin Oriental’s exclusive topper comprises white goose feathers, Waldorf Astoria beds feature a down-alternative fill, and Marriott’s selection is polyester.

There’s no one-size-fits-all here, so it really comes down to your preferred loftiness and weight. Duck and goose feathers are heavier than others fills, though duck is slightly less fluffy and won’t trap heat as well. Down-alternatives, like polyester, are more allergen-friendly and “a good option for those who prefer to be vegan in their home,” Danielle Trotter, the former textiles technical designer at West Elm, previously shared.

What Is the Thickness of a Hotel Mattress?

Hotel mattresses usually average 12 inches in thickness. This makes it easier to hop in and out of bed, especially when using a box spring that can add extra height. Plus, it prevents the need for deep pocket sheets.

How Can I Recreate the Hotel Bed Experience at Home?

We’ve explored the entire topic on how to make your bedroom feel like a hotel, and aside from finding a new bed with a medium-firm feel, we’ve learned that percale sheets and down pillows are pretty much a must to complete the setup. When it comes to the former, hotel sheets are usually made with organic cotton percale because the fabric looks and feels crisp, giving that refined aesthetic a boutique stay is known for. Usually a 200 thread count is a good rule of thumb to look out for since this means there’s plenty of airflow between the threads for a breathable feel. Hotel pillows are usually filled with down feathers since they’re so lofty and soft, but a down alternative is just as good in case you’re an allergy-prone sleeper (just look for materials like hypoallergenic gel fibers since they’re known for being squishy without falling flat, just like a feather-filled pillow).

What Is the Difference Between Memory Foam and Latex?

Traditional memory foam has a body-contouring effect that allows your body to sink into your mattress, reducing motion transfer (a must for bedmates!). Meanwhile, latex foam offers more responsiveness (or bounce) and overall support. As Neslihan Ozdemir, founder of Girl on the Mattress, previously told AD, latex also holds up well over time and is temperature-regulating. Latex foam mattresses (and some memory foam options) are certified organic, making them eco-friendly foam picks, too.

Known as the most common mattress type, innerspring mattresses feature a bed of coils. There’s quite a range to these mattresses: Basic versions have a grid of steel coils, while premier options have a pillow top and pocketed coil technology, meaning each coil is individually wrapped to help with motion isolation. Ozdemir added that innerspring is best for people who sleep on the edge of the bed or are heavier in weight. If you prefer a more plush mattress, but still want the support of those coils, consider a hybrid mattress, which is layered with soft foam.

#4897. Urologists Have Some Hot Takes on Whether Men Should Sit or Stand to Pee

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

AROUND THE WORLD—and on Reddit—there’s an eternal debate raging about whether men should sit or stand to pee. In the US, the answer seems like a no-brainer: standing. One YouGov poll found that only 10 percent of American men regularly sit down to pee, while 31 percent said they never do this. (There’s even that viral video years ago of a pastor arguing “a man is someone who pisses against the wall.”)

But that same YouGov poll found that where you wee varies. In Germany, 40 percent of guys actually sit down every time to urinate. About 22 percent of Swedish men, for example, sit down every time, but 28 percent sit down most of the time. Entire threads online are devoted to this question, including a hybrid tactic as a compromise in which a guy pees sitting down at home but stands up at a urinal in public.

Looking beyond preference, is there a right answer to take a leak? One study published in the journal Neurourology and Urodynamics tried to give a definitive answer. Depending on your camp, the answer might validate what you know—or piss you off.

Researchers had no issue finding 52 guys to sign up for this peeing experiment. These dudes had no prior health issues and were between the ages of 18 and 39. The guys were randomly divided into two groups that sat to urinate. Then they would stand to pee. The other group did the same but in reverse order. Between each change in position was a "washout period" of 24 hours where guys did their business as usual.

Researchers tracked how much urine came out and how quickly. So who reigned supreme on the porcelain throne? Well, neither.

Sitting or standing to urinate didn’t change how much pee they got out in each session. There was a slight difference in how fast they got to max flow, though. Men were able to reach their peak speed slightly sooner when they peed sitting down, but researchers say this finding was “unlikely to be clinically meaningful and was partly dependent on a single outlier.” Meaning, one guy was pissing really hard while sitting, while everyone else peed at a similar rate and volume no matter what position they did it.

The findings are not surprising to S. Adam Ramin, MD, urologist and medical director of Urology Cancer Specialists. “If you're a normal, young, healthy male, it will make no difference whether you sit or stand to urinate,” he says. “You will have a good stream either way.”

THE FINDINGS WOULD likely be different for older men, especially those with an enlarged prostate. “Sometimes in older men with an obstructing prostate, sitting to urinate may help them to empty their bladders more effectively as they are able to generate more abdominal force to squeeze the urine out,” says Boback Berookhim, MD, urologist at Northwell’s Lenox Hill Hospital.

HEALTHWISE, NOT REALLY. But if you have a certain preference for one over the other, then there’s no harm in sticking with one position. There's some convenience with standing to pee: You pull it out, do your business, and move on. Peeing this way is “likely to save time,” says Dr. Berookhim.

Sitters, on the other hand, might prefer the position because it’s slightly more hygienic. Dr. Ramin says guys are more likely to splash, sprinkle on the toilet seat, or even miss entirely when they’re standing versus sitting. Plus, sitters might be more likely to wash their hands after every use. Men are 1.5 times less likely to wash their hands than women after peeing—probably where they could use those saved seconds.

Beyond that necessary bathroom etiquette, there’s really no other reason to switch up your tried-and-true urinary habits. Dr. Berookhim says he certainly wouldn’t tell a young, healthy guy to change the way they are using the bathroom if they are already doing fine.

Dr. Song also recommends swapping out lip balms when seasons change and when you're traveling to a different climate. Use lighter formulas such as Rhode’s Peptide Lip Treatment in warm or humid climates and thicker formulas like the Laneige Lip Mask in cold or dry weather.

Beauty contributors Lily Wohlner and Danielle Jackson joined as testers for this story.

They're all aligned with dermatological guidance and nourish our lips for hours.

#4892. Joseph Dirand Joins Forces with Peter Brant and Stephanie Seymour Brant to Reimagine a Historic 1920s Palm Beach Mansion

It began with a chance encounter and a phone call. The French architect Joseph Dirand was walking into a restaurant in New York when he ran into an old friend, the art dealer Tico Mugrabi. Dirand mentioned that he was flying to Palm Beach the next day and his friend lit up. Mugrabi pulled out his phone and made a call. “Peter, my friend Joseph is coming to Palm Beach tomorrow,” Dirand recalls him saying. “You have to meet this guy.” The following day Dirand was sitting across from Peter Brant, the fabled industrialist and publisher, and his wife, Stephanie Seymour Brant, one of the defining supermodels of her generation, in their new home. The Brants had owned the house for only a few days, and it marked the opening of a new chapter for the couple.

The Brants in front of Warhol’s White Disaster (White Car Crash 19 Times), 1963, in the great room. Jean Prouvé coffee table; sofa and chairs by Pierre Jeanneret.

Marc Newson’s aluminum Lockheed Lounge, a Tower Cabinet by Ettore Sottsass, and a Trapeze table by Jean Prouvé all stand in the loggia.

A Végétale mirror by Claude Lalanne reflects Untitled (Richard Prince and Cindy Sherman), 1980, and a 1930s settee by Jean-Michel Frank.

A pair of bespoke Philippe Anthonioz floor lamps Flank Jonathan Horowitz’s Self-portrait in “Mirror #1” (Kevin), 2012.

Brown Jordan chaise longues under umbrellas by Business & Pleasure Co. stand poolside.

There is something quintessentially American in how quickly it all unfolded, and for Dirand, it meant meeting a man he had long admired. As an inquisitive young designer he had pored over photographs of Brant’s earlier homes, and one image had stayed with him: It showed a Jean Prouvé desk beneath a Jean-Michel Basquiat painting, captured at a time when almost no one thought to set French postwar design against contemporary art. “For me, Peter was a kind of collector’s hero,” says Dirand.

Brant’s eye for art and design was formed early. His father loved classical art and considered even Picasso “way too modern,” but on family ski trips to Switzerland the teenage Brant got to know the Zurich dealer Bruno Bischofberger, who subsequently introduced him to Leo Castelli, and the two titans of the art world became the young Brant’s mentors. Brant then bought his first Andy Warhol painting in 1966, and by the time Warhol’s business manager, Fred Hughes, introduced them in November 1968, he already owned about seven of them. Warhol and Brant would go on to become close friends for the remainder of the artist’s life.

In a corner of the Great Room, Roy Lichtenstein’s The Refrigerator, 1962, faces a 1960 copper hanging cabinet by Paul Evans. a 1934 plaster vase by Alberto Giacometti sits on A Joseph Dirand Edition Iseo Gold coffee table. 1950s Hirondelles wall light by Jean Royère; pair of 1958 Diego Giacometti armchairs.

Warhol’s 1975 portrait of Murray Brant (Brant’s father) commands a wall of the paneled study. Direction armchair and Présidence desk by Jean Prouvé; Ettore Sottsass hanging lamp.

Artworks in the entrance hall include, from left, a Massangis stone lion-head fountain feature by Harumi Klossowska de Rola, 2022; Andy Warhol’s Self Portrait (Green), 1964; a Klossowska de Rola wolf sculpture; and Richard Prince’s Nurses’ Dormitory, 2002. The sanded Ceppo di Gré stone modular console is by Dirand.

In the primary bedroom, George Condo’s 2004 portrait of Stephanie Seymour Brant hangs above a 1946 Charlotte Perriand sideboard on which stands an enameled earthenware lamp by Roger Capron. A Jean Prouvé Bridge armchair joins an Ours Polaire chair and sofa by Jean Royère around Prouvé’s Tripod coffee table.

An exterior view of the 1926 Addison Mizner residence

Few people then saw Warhol’s work the way Brant did. When he hung his first Marilyn at home, visitors were shocked: “People would come to my house and think, This is the worst thing I’ve ever seen. In the 1960s, he says, you could count the serious collectors of Pop art “on three hands.”

His rule, he says, is to collect “something that was in style that’s out of style,” though never as speculation. Between their holdings and those of the Brant Foundation, which he established in 1996 to promote the education and appreciation of contemporary art and design, the collection now numbers more than 3,000 works, and he has never bought for a particular wall. What he misses in many newer collections is any sense of the person behind them. “You can see right away that this guy had a great adviser,” he says, “but there’s no madness in the collection. Every collection should have some madness.”

Carlo Mollino’s Tipo B side chair rests beneath Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Per Capita, 1981.

A painting by Glenn Ligon and a stool by Shiro Kuramata in Brant’s bath

Seymour Brant and Brant in the great room

Brant has shared much of his collecting journey with Seymour Brant, whom he married in 1995. She has built a collection of her own: Her passion is clothing rather than paintings, and she has pursued it with the same scholarship and the same sharp eye as her husband. She was a close friend of the legendary couturier Azzedine Alaïa and has one of the most significant holdings of his work, alongside historic couture that Dirand describes as extraordinary. Where Brant is the storyteller, Seymour Brant is the quieter presence, though Dirand is clear that she was integral to every decision. Her collecting has even changed the way Brant sees his own. “It’s not a dress in a closet,” he says. “It’s a piece of art, and it mixes with art.”

Brant has spent some 50 years in the Palm Beach area, first as a polo player. He and Seymour Brant had no need for a new home there—they loved the one they had as their children grew up. But when Collado Hueco, a home by Addison Mizner, the architect who defined 1920s Palm Beach, came on the market in 2020, the collector in him took over. “It was a piece of history,” Dirand says. “For him, there was no choice.” Designed in 1924 for the American businessman Paul Moore, it is one of Mizner’s boldest and most unusual houses.

In a hall, a 1974 Diego Giacometti bench sits in front of Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Untitled (Sugar Ray Robinson), 1982. The curtain rods are by Julian Schnabel.

Warhol’s The Kiss (Bela Lugosi), 1964, and a 1947 Alexandre Noll mahogany armchair in a corner of the primary bedroom. Philippe Anthonioz hanging light; Jean Prouvé tripod coffee table; Jean Royère Ours Polaire sofa.

John Currin’s Constance Towers, 2009, presides over Seymour Brant’s dressing room. Furniture includes an Ambassador chair and Éléphanteau sofa, both by Jean Royère.

In the great room, a plaster bas-relief, Support, and a carved-stone console by Alberto Giacometti are flanked by a pair of Éléphanteau chairs by Jean Royère. In the foreground is a Fondation Maeght chair by Diego Giacometti.

The house presented Dirand with a real puzzle. Asymmetrical, it spreads across multiple wings, varying from one to three levels. The main entertaining rooms had retained their original character, while the entrance and stair hall were dark and enclosed. Dirand set out to let the sunlight that moves across the house reach every part of the interior as much as possible. The collection shaped Dirand’s approach too. With so many treasured works coming into the house, the team wanted to ensure they would be protected against anything the unpredictable Florida weather could bring. What began as a renovation became, in Dirand’s words, “a reconstruction saving the historical.” Rather than demolishing and starting again, the team kept the historic walls standing, reinforced every one of them, and dug beneath to take the foundations deeper. New hurricane-proof windows were set into concrete frames, the roof was removed and rebuilt, and the original tiles and the patina of the plaster fireplace were carefully preserved. The project took about four years. Throughout, Dirand immersed himself in Mizner’s doors, ceilings, and patterns so that the new rooms would be a true homage rather than a copy.

Early on, Brant handed Dirand two thick binders, one of artworks and one of design pieces. “This is what you can use,” he said. A few days later, on holiday with his family, Dirand spread every page across the floors. “I was walking on the paper,” he says. It reversed the usual order in which the architect designs the rooms and the art arrives afterward. Here the collection came first, though never rigidly, because “a collection is also something that is alive.”

A Diego Giacometti bench and A Jean Royère Liane six-branch floor lamp in a hall

A chair and floor lamp by Diego Giacometti stand next to the fireplace in the great room.

Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Per Capita, 1981, commands a wall of the loggia. Ours Polaire chair and Yo-Yo side table, both by Royère.

A family photo and fragrance bottles line up on a windowsill in Seymour Brant’s bath.

Warhol’s Big Campbell’s Soup Can with Can Opener (Vegetable), 1962, hangs in the stairwell, which also features a Jacques Adnet wall light.

At the heart of the home are two main spaces, the great room and the loggia, which are perhaps the spaces that both Dirand and Brant are most proud of. The great room is centered around a monumental fireplace that has the grandeur of a castle. Commanding one wall is a rare carved-stone console by Alberto Giacometti, nearly three meters high and crowned with a bas-relief of a female figure, made for Jean-Michel Frank’s important 1938 commission for the Born family in Argentina. It was one of a pair, and Dirand says no one knows where the other is today. Beside the fireplace hangs Warhol’s 1963 White Disaster (White Car Crash 19 Times), one of Brant’s most recent and important acquisitions; he had wanted a Car Crash painting since the ’60s. Prouvé furniture from Brazzaville, weathered by the Congo climate, sits amid Native American and African objects, and at the center of it all is a mirror polish copper table Dirand designed himself to reflect Giacometti’s bird vase and the fireplace behind it. Brant calls the table a masterpiece.

Art in the main entrance includes, from left, pieces by Jean-Michel Basquiat, Richard Prince and Cindy Sherman, and Brice Marden. Furniture includes an Ours Polaire Chair and sofa and a kidney-shaped coffee table, all by Jean Royère, and a Charlotte Perriand stool. a 1936 Jean-Michel Frank settee stands in the background.

A glimpse into the primary bedroom, where a Jean-Michel Frank table lamp sits atop a bedside table.

A wall niche holds a 2023 ibis sculpture by Harumi Klossowska de Rola

The loggia is lighter and more playful, and its original black, yellow, and turquoise tiled floor and Egyptian-style column capitals offer a glimpse of Mizner at his most adventurous. One of the most prominent works hanging in the room is a monumental 1981 Basquiat painting, Per Capita, which Brant bought from Annina Nosei’s memorial show for the artist. At the center of the room stands an Ettore Sottsass Tower Cabinet, designed in the early 1960s, which Dirand admits he didn’t understand at first, until Brant showed him exactly how to place it. Now he can’t imagine the room without it.

Upstairs, Dirand took down walls so that the primary bedroom runs the full width of the house, capturing light from sunrise over the ocean to sunset over the garden. In Seymour Brant’s bathroom, Estremoz marble walls are carved to evoke curtains, and beyond it lies her dressing room, an intimate boudoir. Brant’s bathroom, by contrast, is a marquetry of white and gray marble built around a pair of Glenn Ligon paintings. Dirand calls the room “minimalist ornamental.”

A 2023 flamingo sculpture by Harumi Klossowska de Rola (one of a pair) stands on the terrace.

In Seymour Brant’s bath, François-Xavier Lalanne’s Singe II, 1999, sits between a stool by Diego Giacometti and a bespoke bench by Philippe Anthonioz.

Every piece in the house comes with a story, and Dirand heard many of them over years of breakfasts, lunches, and dinners with the couple. “Every single piece could be a book,” he says. During those conversations, the collaboration between Brant and Dirand grew into a close friendship. Brant’s other great passion is horse racing, and his formidable stable has included Sottsass, the 2020 winner of the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe, Europe’s most prestigious race. One day, Brant called Dirand with news: Sottsass had a son, a young thoroughbred already winning races of his own. He had named him Dirand.

With exciting features and a futuristic design, many couldn’t wait to see what the production version would look like.

The prototype spotted in testing is a bit disappointing. Although it’s still disguised, the image from Autohome shows a vehicle that looks very different from the Ocean-V concept earlier this year.

The image shows a boxy design with a wide grille and traditional pull-style door handles, which looks drastically different from BYD’s latest vehicles.

Spotted at a BYD Flash Charger in China, the vehicle was equipped with a massive roof-mounted LiDAR. A video (shown below) of the new model on a car carrier from ThinkerCar offers a closer look.

Local reports suggest the Ocean MPV will be 5,145 mm long, 1,970 mm wide, and 1,805 mm tall, with a 3,045 mm wheelbase. It’s also expected to feature a 2+2+3 seating layout with room for seven passengers.

BYD has yet to confirm any powertrain or battery specs, but given the massive grille up front, the Ocean minivan is expected to use BYD’s DM-i plug-in hybrid system and its Blade Batteries.

BYD’s current MPV lineup includes the Denza D9, a flagship model that starts above 300,000 yuan ($45,000), and the Xia, priced in the 200,000 to 300,000 yuan ($30,000 to $45,000) range. The Ocean MPV is expected to fill the gap.

Zhang Zhou, general manager of BYD’s Ocean series, said the company expects to launch its first MPV by the end of 2026.

#4890. The ‘Midlife Crisis’ Isn’t Real. The Actual Risk Is Believing the Myth.

Knowing the reality can benefit your physical and mental health.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you ask someone what comes to mind when they hear the word midlife, 99.9 percent of the time the answer will be very specific: crisis. Ideas about middle age tend to skew negative, no matter the cause.

As a midlife researcher, this is worrying to me because I know just how pernicious these legacy beliefs can be. Yet the most prevalent negative interpretations of midlife are not supported by the research. The truth is so much more hopeful and, frankly, interesting.

While it’s hard to predict exactly who will experience this, it’s likely that 10 to 20 percent of people in midlife will go through some intense period of challenge and growth. For those folks, it’s important to remember that this isn’t a bad thing. First of all, the “crisis” is only part of the story, and not even the most interesting part. Whatever challenges you face are likely to be followed by changes to your life that will help you become freer, stronger, and more tuned in to what you really want for yourself in the second half of your life.

Debunking the myth of the midlife crisis isn’t just about correcting the record—it’s about harm reduction. Cultural notions have a real-time effect on our perception of our health and well-being in our middle years, and if the “information” is more myth than reality, that can have negative effects on our physical, psychological, and cognitive health.

Research done by Becca Levy, PhD, a professor of public health and psychology at Yale, and summarized in her book Breaking the Age Code, has shown the power of both negative and positive beliefs about aging to impact our healthspan and lifespan. Levy found that those who had more positive images of aging (e.g., being healthy and active) lived longer than those with the more stereotypical views about older adults as weak, forgetful, and slow. She also found that those with a more positive mindset about aging were healthier, with lower blood pressure and a lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease.

Beliefs about aging can eclipse the truth in many arenas. If a woman in her 50s whose children have just left the nest goes to see her physician about feeling excessively fatigued, depressed, and sleepless, the cliché of the midlife crisis makes it more likely that her concerns will be dismissed. This can lead to misdiagnosis for more serious conditions such as depression, autoimmune disorders, or hormonal deficiencies, which if recognized can be treated properly.

One of the best ways to set ourselves up for success when the sea of life starts to get choppy is to pay close attention to the way we are thinking about our story. Whether we know it or not, we are always telling ourselves stories in order to make meaning out of what happens to us and how it makes us feel. When we’re going through a rough patch, it helps immensely to take control of the narrative—moving from a negative frame of mind to a more hopeful one that emphasizes agency and opportunity. On the opposite end of the spectrum from folks who enter midlife ready for battle, many enter midlife on autopilot. Some assume they are stuck with the decisions made early in adulthood. Others want out but don’t imagine the alternatives or can’t see ways to improve circumstances.

Either way, it’s important to remember that it is possible to make tweaks or small changes in midlife; they don’t have to be radical ones. One of my colleagues on the MacArthur Foundation Research Network on Successful Midlife Development used to say, “Some people are so fed up at work that they quit their jobs in frustration, when all they really needed was a two-week vacation.” When we sleepwalk through midlife, at best it’s a missed opportunity for growth, and at worst it simply delays the challenges that will inevitably surface. What we know from the research is that middle age—whether or not you go through a “crisis”—is the time to reflect and make change.

I like to think of midlife as halftime in sports: Some of the important plays have been made, but not all. While a little discomfort with the poor choices of our past isn’t a bad thing, getting mired in regret isn’t something that helps anybody. You have the opportunity to breathe, examine what has come before, and start analyzing what you need to do next to reach your goals or modify them. There is plenty of time left after midlife, so reflection can help people see how they might move in different directions.

For those who don’t know where to begin when it comes to reflecting on their life story and even changing it, there is good research to suggest that a “life review” can help. When done well, a midlife review can help you make sense of the past and bring clarity to your goals moving forward (find out more about how to do it below).

One strategy is to do life reviews at the decade milestones (40, 50, 60) and possibly at the halfway marks (45, 55, 65). Another strategy is to do it when there are significant life events that might require some readjustments, such as going through a divorce, a job loss, or having a child leave home. Midlife is a great time to revisit old stories and even consider some rewrites and new beginnings.

It is important to keep in mind that it is unlikely that you will have accomplished everything you expected to by age 40, 50, or even 60. And it is unrealistic to think you will be happy with all areas of your life. If you think you are having a midlife crisis, ask yourself whether it’s really a crisis or if it’s just that you’re not happy with how some things are going. Maybe it’s just a time to make some changes. The life-shattering, ego-dissembling portrayal of the inescapable midlife crisis we have all become accustomed to is neither inevitable nor universal.

#4888. How One Creative Couple Found Harmony in Their 1920s Los Angeles Craftsman

Nothing about where interior designer Harrison Soll is now was part of the plan. Five years ago, he was focused on his work, and he didn’t want any distractions. But when he met Rodney Burns, a stylist and owner of the legendary Los Angeles vintage gallery, Church Boutique, it set everything on a new path. They met in the fall; by New Year’s they were a couple. “I didn’t think it was going to be a relationship,” Soll says. He credits their shared interests for bringing them together: “We always found a throughline with design.”

They now live in a 1925 craftsman house in Laurel Canyon. Soll took the lead decorating the nearly 1,400-square-foot home in a combination of his and Burns’s styles with many pieces coming from Burns’s eclectic collection of vintage art, furniture, and sculpture. Burns has worked with Lenny Kravitz as a stylist and creative collaborator for the past 15 years, and the singer says he admires what Burns and Soll have created together. “The mix of Rodney’s early- to midcentury style mixed with ethnic expression next to Harrison’s bold minimalist modern approach seamlessly blend together,” Kravitz tells AD.

The backyard of Soll’s and Burns’s Laurel Canyon home is a bricolage of funky, inherited stonework and vintage pottery.

The nail art above the fireplace has a cute backstory story: Burns and Soll had seen it at a vintage shop in Santa Monica and Burns regretted not buying it. When he went back to purchase the piece, it was marked as sold. But only because Soll had already covertly bought it as a Valentine’s Day gift for Burns.

The giant Sergio Bustamante giraffe bust in the foyer is a delicate topic. “The giraffe was one of our biggest fights in decorating this house,” Burns explains. “I was determined to have that giraffe live some place in this house because he’s just fantastic, and the scale of him, and the rarity of him.” Except, counters Soll, that the placement of the giraffe is treacherous because the front door swings right in its path. “You just have to be careful,” Soll says.

The foyer—which features a collection of masks and vintage paintings—was one of the most difficult areas to style, explains Burns. The couple was trying to be selective of what pieces to incorporate from Burns’s massive collection and at one point Burns suggested putting all of his masks in storage to save for another house down the line, or passing them onto Burns’s vintage boutique, Church. Soll dissented, saying, “No, let’s put them everywhere.”

The living room features two sofas—a Joseph D’Urso for Knoll piece reupholstered in leopard fabric and a leather De Sede Terrazza. The carpet is the Antilocarpa style from Stark. A trio of fiberglass shell art was sourced through Kelly Wearstler. The art behind the sofa is a manipulated canvas garment bag by the artist Roosevelt “Rip” Woods, the first black artist to have a solo show at the Phoenix Art Museum.

As renters, there were naturally limitations on what could be achieved. Soll got permission to retile a bathroom and install a new vanity. The doe-patterned wall-to-wall carpeting in the living room was an “ask for forgiveness” move, but his landladies ended up loving it. Burns, on the other hand, needed more convincing. “The carpet took many dinners of conversations between the two of us,” Soll says.

Soll describes himself as more of a minimalist while Burns avows, “I’m a maximalist to the umpteenth power.” The couple attempted to strike a balance while still filling the space with character. Some rooms nod to Soll’s leanings toward minimalism like an office with a midcentury desk and a 1970s tapestry and the dining room where a Sergio Bustamante table and a Chinese Art Deco rug are the main attractions.

When decorating their Laurel Canyon home, Soll and Burns had to figure out how to combine their opposing styles, with Soll being more of a minimalist and Burns being a maximalist. But, says Burns, “[Soll] has made me be able to take a pause and then also make me a little less attached to some of the things that I’ve collected  and given me an opportunity to maybe show a little bit more restraint.” In the corner, a brass Maison Jansen palm tree mingles with a Sergio Bustamante monkey.

Burns, who has been styling Lenny Kravitz for over a decade, says his approach to home design and fashion are one in the same: “Building an outfit, building a room: same thing in my opinion.”

Kravitz offers these kind words on Burns: “What I love about Rodney is that he is limitless in his concepts and always thinks outside of the box. His visual vocabulary enables him to mix a vast stew of eras and genres. He pays tribute to our ancestors and uplifts new innovators. Always soulful, expressive, and elegant.”

In the dining room, Soll placed a Sergio Bustamante table on a diagonal to make enough room for the couple’s large dog. “She’s a girthy girl,” says Soll, referring to the table, not the dog. The chairs are by Paul Evans and the Chinese Art Deco rug was sourced from Ariana Rugs. The Tom Greene chandelier was sourced from Burns’s boutique, Church.

Burns’s maximalism is on display in the living room, where a couch upholstered in leopard Scalamandré mixes with zebra-hide chairs and a sinuous De Sede sofa. (That animal print couch, Soll wants you to know, also features a block of leather upholstery: “I just think it would have been too maximalist to do a full Scalamandré sofa.”)

The living room is filled with brass sculptures (a Maison Jansen palm tree and a Sergio Bustamante monkey), bronze figures sourced from an estate sale in Arizona, and several pieces of sculptural artwork.

The bedroom mixes patterns and textures with a stainless steel bed from TTMM, Paul Evans “Cityscape” nightstands, striped bedding, and antique bronze table lamps with African mud cloth shades.

The 1970s textile art in the office is a vintage find of Burns’s that Soll loves. “I used to go to Rodney’s apartment when we first started dating, and I would be like, ‘Oh my God! Like, if we break up, I’m never gonna be able to find this tapestry,’” he says.

Soll got permission from his landladies to retile the bathroom and add a new vanity. The metal Curtis Jeré artwork comes from Burns’s collection.

The bohemian architecture of the home lends quirkiness to the design. The main bedroom isn’t a perfect square, making it seem like a stainless steel bed from TTMM is placed on a diagonal but is actually following the geometry of a very funky, angular bedroom.

The couple has taken their time tinkering and adjusting the decor, taking a considered approach to collecting and combining their belongings. Soll describes the overall vibe as having an Afrocentric theme that’s also a little bit Ralph Lauren. “Our visions have mingled,” Burns says.

Still, there is one last item the couple needs to complete the design: a blanket basket. But, says Soll, “We still haven’t found one we agree upon.”

The backyard is also home to a shed (not pictured), which functions as Burns’s closet.

#4887. Someone ran Rivian’s pedal-by-wire e-bike out of battery and things got weird

The ALSO TM-B is one of the most technologically interesting new e-bikes to hit the road in years, largely because it does away with one of the most fundamental parts of a bicycle: the mechanical connection between the pedals and rear wheel. With only copper wires connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, the TM-B is one of the most revolutionary new e-bikes in years.

But that raises an obvious question. What happens when the battery dies?

One early Launch Edition owner, Aaron Draczynski, decided to find out by deliberately running his TM-B down toward empty to see whether ALSO’s drive-by-wire system would leave him stranded.

He shared the experience on YouTube, discovering that the answer is surprisingly complicated – and involves something called “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Unlike a conventional e-bike, where the rider’s pedaling mechanically turns the rear wheel through a chain or belt, the ALSO TM-B uses a pedal-by-wire drivetrain. Pedaling generates electricity, while the rear wheel is driven electrically.

That arrangement enables all sorts of interesting features, including electronically simulated gearing and the Launch Edition’s massive Level 10 boost mode, which can multiply rider input by up to 10 times.

But it also means there’s no traditional drivetrain to fall back on when the battery runs out.

Fortunately, the bike doesn’t simply go from full power to dead.

The owner began his experiment at 31% charge and quickly watched the bike progressively restrict its maximum assist as the battery drained closer to empty. From 23% to 13%, the maximum boost dropped from Level 8 to Level 5 as it began conserving battery.

By 10% charge, the bike was limited to Level 4. At 8%, it dropped to Level 3, followed by Level 2 at 5%. Shortly afterward, only Level 1 remained. Then at 4% battery, conventional electric assistance disappeared entirely.

Interestingly, the normal electronic shifting of the bike’s simulated software gears continued to work through most of that process. But when the battery reached 4%, things changed as the bike started exhibiting issues. The first sign of trouble came when the bike began seemingly randomly shifting gears while in manual mode without the rider even touching the shifter. Several times per second, the bike seemed to want to shift itself between gears.

Keep in mind that the TM-B doesn’t have actual physical gears (and no chain or derailleur, for that matter), but instead simulates various gears using predefined software to make the rider feel like they are working more or less intensely to pedal the bike.

Once the TM-B reached its final low-battery state, an infinity symbol appeared on the display and the bike entered what the owner referred to as “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Instead of using stored battery energy to provide meaningful assistance, the system effectively attempts to pass the rider’s pedaling energy through the electronic drivetrain to keep the rear wheel turning. It’s similar in concept to those old crank-powered flashlights, which, even with a dead storage battery, would still illuminate for as long as the owner cranked them.

And on flat ground, the owner reported that the infinite turtle mode apparently worked surprisingly well.

Draczynski described the experience as roughly equivalent to pedaling a normal bicycle in fourth gear. There was resistance at the pedals, and he could maintain a reasonable pace without feeling like he was simply spinning his legs uselessly.

Then he reached a hill and found the limitation of that effectiveness. Even a slight incline transformed the experience, with the bike feeling more like it was permanently stuck in seventh or eighth gear. Getting home through his hilly neighborhood became, in his words, a “truly grueling ordeal.”

Manual shifting was also disabled in this mode, meaning there was no way to electronically select an easier virtual gear for climbing, since again, there aren’t any physical gears in the bike. Everything in the pedaling experience is software-simulated.

That’s an important limitation for a bike relying entirely on a drive-by-wire drivetrain. The infinite turtle mode might keep you moving with significant effort on level terrain, but it doesn’t turn a dead TM-B into a conventional bicycle, unless that conventional bicycle is being ridden through beach sand.

The low-power state apparently shuts down some other features as well. The owner could no longer lock or unlock the TM-B through ALSO’s smartphone app, though he did report the bike’s touchscreen controls continued working, and he guessed that the bike had shut down connectivity to conserve power for its key systems to operate.

Perhaps more concerning than the low-battery riding experience was what happened when this particular TM-B was simply sitting in the owner’s garage.

Describing another scenario he encountered, Draczynski says he left the bike sitting unplugged in his garage at around 70% charge. The following evening, it had fallen to 40%, and a day later it was down to 18%.

When he returned the next morning, the TM-B displayed a “Bike issue detected” message followed by “Install battery to ride.”

There was just one problem: the battery was already installed.

Plugging in the charger didn’t initially help because the bike apparently couldn’t detect its own battery, and thus charging didn’t begin. Worse, the battery refused to eject using the normal ejection process, leaving the owner unable to remove it and charge it off of the bike.

Ultimately, Draczynski used the physical reset button underneath the frame, which brought the system back to life. The bike recognized the battery again and began charging normally.

Much like modern EVs, I would imagine a lot of these issues will be fixed via a software update. Early adoption is fun but you’re basically beta testing a product for the company at full price.

That degree of overnight battery drain obviously isn’t something we’d expect from a normal e-bike, so hopefully this was either an isolated software issue or something ALSO can address with an update. For his part, Draczynski suspects that the bike might be draining its battery so heavily at rest due to the lack of a cell signal in his garage. “I was quite surprised at the drop from day to day,” he explained on Reddit. “If I had to wager a guess, the bike might be searching for a cellular signal, but there’s no reception in my garage so it’s just draining the battery.”

But the experiment offers an interesting first real-world look at one of the biggest questions surrounding ALSO’s unusual drivetrain.

A normal e-bike with a dead battery becomes a heavy bicycle. The TM-B instead becomes something much stranger: an electricity-generating exercise machine that uses your legs to generate current, electronically sends that current through the bike, and then uses it to turn the rear wheel.

And based on this testing, it does in fact work. Just try not to be at the bottom of a hill when you find out for yourself.

#4886. The 7 Best Firming Body Lotions for Tightening Skin, Tested by Experts

Editors gave top marks to formulas from Nivea and Charlotte Tilbury.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Skin changes are part of life—thanks to sun exposure, the natural dip in collagen and elastin once you hit your late 20s, or shifts in weight (hi, pregnancy!). So if your skin doesn’t quite have the same snap-back it once did, that’s completely normal. The good news? You don’t need pricey lasers or an intense 10-step routine to see a difference. The right body-firming lotion can help skin look plumper, smoother, and more resilient.

Firming body lotions can offer smoother, tighter, and less dimpled skin. While nothing can compare to the results you may get from an in-office procedure—topicals aren’t going to work miracles, after all—you might be surprised at just how far hydration can improve the appearance of crepey skin. “The physical transformation of hydration can be profound on our skin,” says dermatologist Nava Greenfield, MD. “The skin will actually appear plumper when a lotion used to ‘firm’ is applied. Adding nutrients to the skin on a consistent basis can also help in creating a healthy, firm appearance.”

Like other categories of skincare products, some firming formulas will always be better than others. To help streamline your shopping experience, I asked dermatologists for their expertise on how to shop for body lotions, along with product recommendations.

For the past few months, beauty contributor Danielle Blundell and I have been researching and testing the best firming lotions. After consulting six dermatologists for their shopping guidance, we asked for their no-fail recommendations as a starting point. We got our hands on some of these picks and shared our testing feedback to help you determine which option works for your unique beauty needs. And to ensure there was a variety of firming body lotions across all budgets, we spent hundreds of hours vetting products for their ingredient list, formulation, absorbency, long- and short-term hydration and firming benefits, and pricing. Of the dozens we tested, these were the best ones we’re willing to auto-refill.

So, get ready for smoother, tighter, and, yes, firmer skin.

Given the fast-acting results Blundell experienced, and the impressive ingredient list we knew the Nivea Skin Toning Gel-Cream was our best overall option. When looking at price, packaging size, and the strength of a given formula’s ingredients, this lightweight cream is hard to beat.

The combination of antioxidant Coenzyme Q10, which aids in cell turnover, and L-carnitine, a chemical known to bolster skin energy reserves and oxygen consumption in skin cells, packs a firming and hydrating punch that’ll leave your skin feeling silky-smooth. We saw improved tightness in just two weeks with twice daily use, and you can choose between almond and lotus scents depending on your preferences for fragrances.

Blundell loves the gel-like texture of this one—it’s a little bit runny right out of the tube, but it sinks into her skin with minimal rubbing and goes on with a bit of a cooling sensation, which feels especially refreshing in the mornings before work and during any waterfront vacations you’re taking. Hours after a quick application (and even a SoulCycle class and quick shower later), Blundell’s legs looked slightly more taut and still felt supple to the touch, as though she had just put the lotion on.

Sometimes the best products are the ones you’ll use religiously. To that end, you can slather on this lotion morning, noon, and night, thanks to its under $10 price tag and light-but-creamy texture that’s easy to apply. Blundell saw results like immediate hydration, but it took three weeks to notice less crepey skin.

“Although the role of topical collagen isn't fully understood yet, this product contains a hydrating form of vitamin B3, niacinamide, and a form of B5 panthenol, which strengthen skin and improve skin quality,” says Dr. Nazarian. “It also absorbs really nicely and applies easily and quickly, making it a great and affordable option for improving skin health.”

Dr. Sartor mentions the lotion does include a nice mix of moisturizers (petrolatum, stearic acid) to prevent water loss as well as antioxidants (niacinamide, tocopheryl acetate) for firming benefits, especially for its cost. “It also contains free fatty acids (palmitic acid) to repair the skin barrier,” she adds.

The only downside for the price? The formula contains a synthetic fragrance, so if you have sensitive skin, you might want to skip it for that reason.

Why settle for just skin firming on your body when you enjoy it on your face as well? This 2-in-1 lotion earned major snaps from dermatologist Dr. Lauren Penzi, MD, for that reason. "It has a powerful retinol and peptide complex that exfoliates to support the skin's renewal process," she says. That means it’ll go to work on discoloration and fine lines on your face and body while you sleep, since it’s a night treatment.

She highlights the intensive humectant and emollient moisturizers and vitamins that keep the skin hydrated for 24 hours as essential for skin firming and smoothing. You can see that in the texture; it’s rich and thick but still rubs in easily and dries quickly, so it’s not a pain to put on before bed.

A great place to give it a go first might be the neck and chest, where wrinkles tend to start popping up sooner than we all might like. Just keep in mind your skin type. Women with oily or combination skin might find it a tad heavy, so start with a pea-sized amount on the face and only add more as needed. Those with normal or dry skin will love this one due to its wonderfully hydrating formula.

Although Revision is a pricey pick, Dr. Nazarian argues it’s well worth the splurge because of the science-backed results and clinical trials. “It combines a cocktail of peptides and antioxidants to promote collagen, prevent breakdown, and ingredients like glucosamine to support cell turnover.” In other words, this product will help tighten loose skin.

BodiContour can be used before and after professional treatments to help enhance your results. However, you should wait until any broken skin is fully healed after your procedure before incorporating this cream back into your routine.

Dr. Sartor likes the hyaluronic acid in the formula as well but notes that the lotion is part of a three-step regimen. She thinks the brand’s promised results—from the fading of sun damage to the tightening of dimply, saggy skin—will be seen with use of the entire system. And even if a little lotion does go a long way, the instructions do recommend applying it twice a day and exfoliating twice a week. So with that does come a significant investment of time and money.

It's not called Magic Cream for nothing. This silky body cream blends caffeine and hydrating all-star hyaluronic acid to smooth and firm the skin. "It also includes the iconic magic 8 matrix, which includes vitamin C and E, aloe vera, camellia oil, rosehip oil, and shea butter, plus moisturizing frangipani flower extract," says dermatologist Dr. Marisa Garshick, MD. "Together this helps to brighten the skin and leave the skin glowing."

Of all the formulas Blundell tried, the Magic Body Cream is the one that left the most noticeable sheen and slight blurring effect on her skin. Putting it on feels luxurious, too; it’s rich but not so heavy that it doesn’t blend well, and it has a similar fragrance to its sister product, Magic Cream anti-aging face moisturizer. The only downside? At $65 a pop, it’s expensive, so Blundell saves it for nights when she’s showing a little skin or wants to target visible areas like the arms, legs, and tummy when sporting resort wear.

StriVectin is well regarded as a top-tier line for anti-aging and skin-firming products, and this rich body cream is a shining example of why the brand has a cult-like following among beauty insiders. And it all starts with the ingredients. A combination of turmeric root and jojoba seed extracts paired with a buttery blend of shea, murumuru, and cupuacu provide deep moisture to improve the look of skin texture and crepiness, says dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD. The turmeric helps brighten uneven skin tone while peptides and jojoba seed extract work together to tighten the skin and make it appear visibly more firm.

If you’re looking to fight back against particularly crepey arms or kneecaps, Dr. Sartor points out that this formula does include more antioxidants than some of the less expensive drugstore options. She also highlights the caffeine and collagen peptides, which work in tandem with the other firming extracts mentioned above. “This would be a good option for more mature skin in need of a richer moisturizer with more skin benefits,” she says.Although spending $44 might seem like a lot, there are other luxury anti-aging lotions out there selling for $165 to $220. If it helps, each container will last around 6 to 12 weeks, depending on how often you apply and if you’re slathering all over or just targeting a smaller area of your body. Regardless, even if you buy a few replacements in the year at $176, you get a year’s worth of product for significantly less than if you were splurging on a single high-end firming body lotion.

If you’re looking for an ultralight, gel-like product that can smooth, plump, and deliver silky-to-the-touch skin, then Nécessaire The Body Serum is the best pick for you. The formula is made with gentle clean ingredients that don’t skimp on quality. It combines ceramides with five molecular weights of hyaluronic acid which provides multilevel hydration. The result: a plumping finish that delivers a bit of lift and tautness. Glycerin further moisturizes the skin, while aloe vera calms redness and irritation. There’s also niacinamide for fine line-fighting benefits.

I’ve been using this serum on and off for a few years, and I can confidently attest to its effectiveness. It helps clear up eczema flare-ups, and has been a beauty lifesaver during the winter when it’s freezing outdoors and my radiator is cranked up inside. A single layer of the clear serum soaks into my skin in seconds, and if your skin is extra parched like mine is then you can apply additional layers as needed without pilling or leaving behind a sticky mess. It’s a year-round must-have for me because in the spring and summer I can just get away with using this instead of a thick lotion or cream.

“This serum does not have any firming ingredients but instead contains hyaluronic acid to plump skin appearance and ceramides to repair the skin barrier,” says Dr. Sartor. “This serum also contains lecithin to help prevent further water loss from the skin surface.”

Honestly, the only downside with this serum is that it’s fragrance-free. Nécessaire does fragrances so incredibly well that I wish they extended their enticing aromas into The Body Serum as well. Still, I fully stand by this serum and if you’re on the fence give it a go and see for yourself. With Amazon Prime’s signature two-day shipping and a 30-day money-back guarantee you have extra reassurance to treat yourself.

You’ve probably been using body lotion since middle school, and firming formulas look and feel roughly the same. They’re applied the same way, too; just massage a dollop into the skin, let it dry for a bit, and you’re good to go on with your day. A few key features, though, are what can separate a good option from a great one, and this is what you’ll want to consider when shopping for the best firming body lotions.

For dermatologist Dr. Rachel Nazarian, MD, certain ingredients are a must if you’re looking to tone and improve the skin’s texture.

Ultimately, whatever lotion, oil, serum, or cream you choose comes down to your skin’s needs. On the most basic level, sometimes it’s just a matter of texture preference—maybe you like the lightness of an oil or serum and want to go that route, or the richness of a cream is what you gravitate toward in the colder months. But some skin types really do fare better with certain formats over others, so you’ll want to keep that in mind.

Serums, gels, and lotions are lightweight and generally better suited for women under 40 with normal or acne-prone skin. Because they’re not heavy, they’re also fantastic if you have sensitive skin all over. You can follow it up with a cream as spot treatment in areas like your kneecaps and elbows that require more moisturization, says Dr. Sartor.

Creams are thick and deeply hydrating, making them helpful for dry and mature skin. You can also use them if you have sensitive skin. However, there is a trade-off. Hyaluronic acid penetrates the skin more easily in lighter serums and gels, so you might need to choose between a gentler product and a more effective moisturizer.

Though not as important as ingredients or format, size can matter when it comes to choosing a firming body lotion, mainly because it can factor into a product’s price and usage. If you want to make a smaller, more expensive lotion go further, consider applying it to target areas—think the butt, thighs, tummy, or upper arms. Consistency is key, though, so a product that you can use more frequently could be better than something you’d have to use sparingly.

Dr. Nava Greenfield, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist at Schweiger Dermatology Group in New York City.

Dr. Rachel Nazarian MD, FAAD, is a board-certified dermatologist with Schweiger Dermatology Group in New York City.

Dr. Quynh-Giao Sartor, MD, FAAD, is a board-certified dermatologist at Westlake Dermatology in Houston, Texas.

Dr. Lauren Penzi, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist at MDCS Dermatology: Medical Dermatology & Cosmetic Surgery in New York.

Dr. Marisa Garshick, MD, FAAD, is a board-certified dermatologist and assistant clinical professor of dermatology at Cornell - New York Presbyterian Medical Center.

Dr. Brendan Camp, MD, FAAD, is a board-certified dermatologist at MDCS Dermatology in New York.

It’s important to manage your expectations for firming lotions—they’re not the cure-all for sagging skin. Severe laxity and deep folds aren’t going to disappear overnight, but your skin will perk up and even plump a bit temporarily upon application.

“You can expect to see your skin slowly showing fewer fine lines and less sag,” says Dr. Greenfield. “A firming cream also has the potential to introduce nutrients that allow your skin to feel smoother and more supple.”

Proper timing is key for absorption and even application, so do yourself a favor and apply right after you’ve just bathed so it sinks in easily, especially if you’re only using this kind of product once a day.

“It is best to apply body lotion when your skin is still damp from a shower but not wet,” says Dr. Greenfield. “Towel dried is optimal. After exfoliating, it is crucial to apply a moisturizer. Best results will ultimately be with consistent and liberal use.”

“Creams are not capable of the same type of tightening that lasers and surgical options can offer,” says Dr. Nazarian. “Despite this, with consistent, continued use, you can certainly see improvement in laxity over time.” But again, commitment to regular use will impact results because everyone’s skin is fighting an uphill battle to a certain extent, at least when it comes to the loss of skin firmness and volume. For the best results, you have to commit to using one regularly to improve the quality of skin laxity, says Dr. Nazarian.

The short answer is yes—but with the caveat that it’s possible to have some kind of a reaction to any body lotion or cream. “Most of these body firming lotions have very little risk,” says Dr. Nazarian. “They are often directed to be used daily, some even twice a day. Major risks include irritation from one of the ingredients or a potential allergy to one of the ingredients.”

Just steer clear of anything with retinol in it, if you’re nursing or pregnant, and discontinue use of a product you have a negative reaction to. “Occasionally, people may experience drying of their skin, especially if the ingredients have the ability to decrease oil production, such as with retinol,” says Dr. Nazarian. “Monitor for those changes and decrease use if they are noted.”

#4884. Harley-Davidson’s electric motorcycle brand LiveWire warns it may not survive

Harley-Davidson-born electric motorcycle maker LiveWire has issued a troubling warning about its financial future, announcing that it has substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating as a going concern. The news sent LiveWire’s stock plunging more than 40% on Thursday morning as the company withdrew its full-year financial guidance.

The announcement comes despite some signs of improving sales, with LiveWire reporting a 38% increase in third-quarter revenue to $7.9 million and a 21% rise in motorcycle unit sales. However, the company continues to burn through cash, reporting a net loss of $18.6 million for the quarter.

LiveWire’s cash reserves have also dwindled significantly, falling from $82.8 million at the end of 2025 to just $39.9 million as of September 30, 2026.

The company has now formed a special restructuring committee to explore potential financing arrangements, strategic partnerships, investments, or even a sale. It also withdrew its previous guidance projecting a $70 million to $80 million operating loss for 2026.

The financial warning comes at a particularly pivotal moment for LiveWire, which is preparing to launch its most affordable electric motorcycles yet.

The upcoming LiveWire S4 Honcho series represents a major departure from the company’s existing premium electric motorcycles, offering smaller, lighter, and significantly more affordable models designed to attract a much broader audience of riders with a starting price below US $5,000.

The lower prices could dramatically increase LiveWire’s sales volumes, especially as the company attempts to move beyond the relatively small market for high-dollar electric motorcycles. The Honcho lineup is also expected to help lower the barrier to entry for new riders, with approachable electric motorcycles that eliminate the complexity of clutch and gear shifting.

LiveWire is also preparing to showcase its latest developments at EICMA in Milan next week, where it is expected to display new models and further expand its upcoming electric motorcycle lineup.

Whether those new motorcycles can arrive quickly enough to turn around the company’s financial situation remains to be seen.

This is genuinely sad news to see. If there’s any legacy motorcycle manufacturer that deserves to succeed in the electric motorcycle space, it’s Harley-Davidson.

Make all the jokes you want about old dudes in leather jackets riding around on loud, chrome-covered motorcycles. But the fact is that Harley-Davidson was taking electric motorcycles seriously when most other major motorcycle manufacturers were still pretending they didn’t exist.

Harley-Davidson didn’t just dip its toes into electric motorcycles. It dove in headfirst, developing the original LiveWire electric motorcycle well over a decade ago and eventually bringing a highly acclaimed production bike to market in 2019. That’s right, Harley-Davidson had a legitimately impressive electric motorcycle on the road before COVID was even a thing. Meanwhile, most of its legacy competitors are only now starting to roll out their first serious electric offerings.

Maybe it's news to Electrek, but while Harley was contemplating electric motorcycles, Zero was selling them for over a decade and continues to do so. There are some high end bikes that Livewire just didn't compete with yet cost $30k when it first came out damaging the brand perception. Newer, lower priced models don't help.

There is also competition from run around eScooters that are way cheaper even cheaper than upcoming Honcho.

And that’s what makes this so frustrating. Harley-Davidson did the hard part. It invested early, developed excellent technology, received rave reviews, and proved that electric motorcycles could be thrilling, premium machines. But building great motorcycles and building a profitable electric motorcycle business have turned out to be two very different challenges.

The timing is especially unfortunate because I genuinely believe LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho series could be exactly what the company needs. These smaller, significantly more affordable electric motorcycles could finally open LiveWire up to a younger audience that doesn’t have $15,000 to drop on a flagship motorcycle but still wants something fun, stylish, and electric for $5,000.

In many ways, that audience seems like a much more natural fit for LiveWire’s branding and ethos than the premium motorcycle market it has been chasing for years.

I really hope LiveWire can find what it needs to get through this difficult period. After spending more than a decade helping drag the legacy motorcycle industry kicking and screaming into the electric age, it would be a real shame to see the company stumble just as its most promising chapter might be about to begin.
