TBH, finding a red light LED face mask that’s under $300 is rare, let alone a reputable model that’s under $100. Despite the low price, dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD, endorses this mask as an impressive, budget-friendly option. Both Dr. Camp and Underwood appreciate the various light modes—red, blue, and amber—that target wrinkles, acne, and inflammation. Underwood considers it an especially great option for women with mature skin concerned with wrinkles and younger users battling breakouts.

Its pretty pink design is cute, but the lightweight feel—especially compared to the Qure—and wireless design are equally impressive. You can glow up while completing chores or watching an episode of Curb Your Enthusiasm which is super practical since treatments last up to 30 minutes.

Despite the affordable price tag, it's a lighter option than Qure's mask (one versus two pounds) and features built-in eye protection (rimmed glasses built into the mask) so you don't have to struggle to get the eye protection to fit.

On the downside, the lights sit slightly further away from the face and don't appear as bright as others we tried even though the nanometers listed in the manual are comparable. That said, you’re only paying $99 for this mask, which is only a third of other alternatives on this list, so the trade off isn’t that bad.

If you're on the hunt for a red light therapy tool that checks all of the boxes (who isn't?!), Qure's Light Therapy Mask is a solid answer—and one that will help you reap a lifetime of benefits. In addition to two types of red light—red and deep red—for anti-aging benefits, the mask also boasts infrared, amber, and blue lights to deal with acne, fine lines, and sun spots.

Using the device is simple: Hold down the power button for three seconds until the light turns on, adjust the straps, and press the button once for the anti-aging mode or press it twice for the acne treatment. You can also use the smartphone app to customize a plan just for you. The icing on the cake? Treatment time is only three minutes for all plans—among the fastest of all the devices we tested.

Qure's various LED lights are within the correct wavelength range to treat multiple skin concerns. For example, acne-fighting blue light should be between 400 and 500nm (Qure's is 415nm), while near-infrared is most helpful between 760 and 1,400nm.

In our evaluations, Earley loved the structure of the mask, which sits squarely on her face so it doesn’t need to be constantly readjusted (an annoying feature of some of the others we tried). "This mask is lightweight, and fit my face perfectly, making me feel like I was reaping the most benefits," says Earley.

The upfront investment for the Qure device has been well worth it for Metzger, who tested the Qure Light Therapy Mask for three weeks. "It’s simple, fast, and effective enough to become a daily habit—and that consistency is everything [when] it comes to skincare,” she said in her review. Metzger considers it an excellent complement to her skincare routine and is a proactive way for her to address her mature skin concerns.

On the downside, the customization component overcomplicated things, said Metzger. Qure has a compatible smartphone app that’s useful, but Metzger admitted it has a learning curve. “I found tinkering with it to be too time-consuming and defeated my favorite aspects of simplicity and speed," she said. This isn’t a huge dealbreaker for Metzger since she enjoys using the standard anti-aging mode.Qure LED Face Mask Review

Boasting a 4.1-star average from nearly 1,300 Amazon reviews—780 are perfect 5-star ratings—this popular red light therapy tool is worth owning, according to Men’s Health associate health and fitness editor Jocelyn Solis-Moreira. She wasn’t eager to spend a few hundred dollars on an LED face mask, but the price tag of the Pure Daily Care Luma Mask was too good to pass up.

Unlike pricier options—such as Dr. Dennis Gross—Amazon’s favorite LED face mask emits seven LED lights to target everything from wrinkles and hyperpigmentation to acne and dullness. Though she had seven light settings to choose from, she stuck with the red wavelengths to target her skin concerns for a full month. She saw results starting in week two—her complexion was more radiant and less puffy. She could also adjust the light intensity, making the Luma Mask helpful for anyone who might be light-sensitive.

The setup instructions were easy for Solis-Moreira to follow. “I love that they idiot-proofed it. All I had to do was connect three pieces,” she says. Solis-Moreira adds that the elastic band was super helpful for keeping her device locked in place.

That said, there are some minor cons. “Though the mask was inflexible—honestly, I felt like Iron Man with it on,” she says. Since it was so rigid, it did not mold to her face. Another downside? The mask sat heavily on her eyebrows, and the lip cutout was too low, so she had to occasionally adjust it. Still, for the price point, these weren't dealbreakers. The mask was relatively comfy enough that Solis-Moreira dozed off with the unit on during her three 20-minute weekly sessions. Don’t worry: it automatically powers down after each setting, making it practical for busy women looking for skin benefits without overthinking the process.

Crunched for time? Same! In just three minutes, Solawave emits a powerful blend of four LED wavelengths—red, near-infrared, deep red, and amber—to smooth lines on my décolletage. The mask features a high density of LEDs—320 to be exact—meaning my skin is basking in vibrant wavelengths with minimal gaps for ample coverage. After a month, my skin is glowing. No wonder I named it the best LED mask of 2026 in our annual Beauty Awards!

So what else makes Solawave the hot topic of my group chat? Many brands sell LED masks only for the chest, but Solawave covers both my décolletage and neck. TBH, I expected it to feel uncomfy around my neck, kinda like a tight choker. However, its lightweight feel and silicone material are surprisingly comfortable. There’s also an adjustable neck strap to customize the fit.

While the pretty pink design doesn’t enhance the functionality, it does look like a tool Elle Woods from Legally Blonde would own, and that’s honestly just an extra perk for me.

Honestly, the only con is the time commitment. Collagen production begins to decline in your mid-20s, but it’s a gradual process. So if you’re younger, it’s more about prevention versus reducing crepey skin. If you’ve lived a full life with wonderful memories and gained wisdom (lucky you!). This device is still worth using—I saw a literal glow-up within my first month of use, and it only got better with time.

Boasting a 4.5/5 star rating from nearly 350 reviews, this red light therapy device is beloved by Amazon shoppers for its ability to offer cosmetic benefits and support your at-home recovery.

This tool is unique because it boasts an overhead display of 287 rows of light diodes and a 180-degree light source that provides a nearly 360-degree treatment for your face, neck, hands, and body. Its design is most similar to something you might see in a salon or dermatologist setting and features the most light options on our list: red, blue, green, cyan, purple, yellow, and white.

Yellow LED light therapy reduces redness and inflammation, improves skin tone and texture, and potentially minimizes the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles, all while promoting skin cell rejuvenation, says dermatologist and dermatopathologist Amy Spizuoco, DO. Purple LED light therapy combines red and blue light, meaning it offers benefits, like acne treatment, reduced inflammation, and improved overall skin health, making it a versatile option for skincare, says Dr. Spizuoco. Lastly, she highlights the unique white LED as a win since it uses the full spectrum of visible light which reduces fine lines and evens skin tone.

One of the best benefits of a panel like this is that you can use it on different areas of your body if you’re dealing with back or chest acne. It’s also helpful for treating and preventing wrinkles on your neck and décolletage. You can also use red light to benefit athletic performance, and this panel emits 640nm of red light to target sore muscles and swelling to do just that.

According to the brand, you only have to use it two to three times per week to see a difference—a smaller commitment than the three to five times a week many other brands suggest. Given the panel design, it’s also more comfortable than rocking an LED mask since you lay down on your couch or bed and place it over your face. That said, if you're the type to multitask during red light therapy treatments, you'd probably favor a mask to this panel because it’s not hands-free and doesn’t have eye holes with protective shields.

The TheraFace Pro offers just about everything: multiple types of light therapy, percussive massage, microcurrent skin-toning, and cleansing. It's all possible thanks to eight different attachments that adhere to the head of the device via powerful magnets.

The highly versatile pick garnered high praise from Wohlner, but it didn't land our top spot because it's not hands-free, so we couldn’t take advantage of multitasking or the flexibility to relax during treatments. Zitz is also a big fan of her Theraface Pro, which she's been using on a weekly basis for two years. She says it's been a game-changer for at-home facials and loves that she can easily switch between red, blue, and infrared light therapy.

If you don't mind manually holding the device to your face, Wohlner says it offers an excellent value. She uses it to treat persistent acne or redness. And using the device is incredibly easy. Wohlner snaps on the blue or red light rings and watches her zits shrink within a week. The percussive therapy also relieves Wohlner’s jaw tension caused by grinding her teeth.

Unfortunately, the brand doesn't list exact treatment time, which makes the process a little ambiguous. However, Wohlner uses the device for about eight minutes. Start at the center of the chin and glide with light pressure upward to your right ear, then slide it back and forth until you finish each quadrant of your face. She wishes the directions were a bit clearer here, but if you want a truly multipurpose device, then this is the one for you.

Although this pick is expensive, it’s FDA-cleared and built to last for years, says dermatologist Shari Sperling, DO. She appreciates that it's equipped with both blue light for acne and red for aging skin. Unlike other models on this list—Skin Gym Wrinklit Mask and Revlit Wand—you can even use both lights simultaneously to treat aging skin and blemishes, making it one of the most customizable choices on this list. This versatility is especially enticing for women in their 40s dealing with hormonal breakouts during perimenopause and menopause.

Still, the quick treatment time of just three minutes makes it a cinch to fit into your busy life. And FWIW, DeSantis tested this mask consistently for a month and found it seamlessly integrated into her routine. The shape hugs the contours of her face like a glove and doesn’t feel like a chore to wear, she said in her review. DeSantis said the treatments were so fast that she would leave the mask on after the lights turned off and she’d continue journaling, scrolling social media, or watching TV.

That said, there is a con to keep in mind: The LED mask sits close to the face despite its more structured design. On the downside, it's a bit heavier than the Qure mask, which means it can become cumbersome after multiple wears, and the high price tag may deter some. While it’s an upfront investment, using this device for a month will still be cheaper than trekking to your dermatologist for an initial treatment and weekly upkeep.

Read more: Dr. Dennis Gross LED Face Mask Review

Dr. Patel and facial plastic surgeon Konstantin Vasyukevich, MD, recommend this mask, which features flexible silicone that molds to all face shapes and sizes—a huge plus for wearability and comfort. Our beauty contributors are also fans of this. Earley enjoyed its flexibility because it’s easier to use than the other options she's tried.

Our testers—Earley, Wohlner, and Zitz—committed to a six-week testing window. They completed each 10-minute session three times a week and were pleased with the results. Wohlner’s discoloration slowly disappeared and her dull complexion became brighter. Zitz appreciates how comfortable the soft silicone material is to wear and says it helps reduce acne and post-acne marks with regular use.

We are also impressed that Omnilux Contour combines red 633nm and near-infrared 830nm lights for major anti-aging benefits. A 2021 study found that a combination of red and near-infrared lights helps boost collagen production and reduce fine lines and wrinkles.

While this face mask earned snaps from our experts, it doesn’t come with built-in eye protection. Since the red light glowed through the eye holes, Earley said it distorted her vision a bit—especially if she was trying to do something else, like make breakfast. You could lounge on your couch or bed for 10 minutes with your eyes closed instead of reading a book or scrolling TikTok. But, your safest bet is to read the manual and heed Omnilux’s eye protection instructions.

What makes this tool stand out? It combines red, acne-fighting blue, and green LED light to reduce inflammation and fade hyperpigmentation. And this palm-sized device glides effortlessly on your face and body. All you need is three minutes a day to minimize wrinkles.

Glide the Skin Gym device across your face to enjoy the same complexion-enhancing benefits of an LED face mask or use it on your neck, chest, and arms to smooth lines and target concerns like bacne, hyperpigmentation, and sunspots.

Each light is designed to be used separately, but Dr. Camp suggests using the green light last because it soothes inflammation and irritated skin. According to dermatologist Kiran Mian, MD, green light also targets surface-level redness, so if rosacea is an issue, this mode is worth integrating into your routine.

I've got a great list of options for you, but if you find yourself in the market for a red light therapy tool, here are a few things to keep in mind.

There are several kinds of red light therapy devices to choose from, including panels, masks, and facial wands, and one may be a better fit for you based on your lifestyle and the area you're seeking to treat.

LED masks are the most common variety you'll find for home use because most are hands-free and contain a lot of diodes (a fancy way of referring to the individual light sources), offering a burst of light to treat the face, neck, or chest.

Maybe you're claustrophobic and the idea of wearing masks gives you the heebie-jeebies—that's where panels come in. They look like flexible bodyboards that you lie down under, and they come in a diverse range of shapes and sizes, each offering different levels of red light exposure to your face, décolletage, and back. These also help replace the need for a separate lip-specific red light therapy tool.

Wands are appealing when you want to target smaller specific areas (the crow's feet or smile lines, for example) and like to do your treatments on the go (you can walk around while using these).

Our eyes are the first place to show signs of aging, so you’ll want to take a cue from dermatologist Pooja Rambhia, MD, and use these affordable red light therapy eye tools. They target fine lines, wrinkles, darkness, and puffiness early on, making them a smart preventive beauty move.

It's tempting to pick a device with the quickest treatment window, especially if you don't have loads of free time to sit back and chill with a red light mask. But remember: To treat more advanced signs of aging, a longer treatment time may be more beneficial. Look at the full picture before you base your purchase on the convenience of a quicker treatment. And for what it’s worth, almost all of our featured recommendations can be used in just three minutes, so even busy women can incorporate quick treatments into their routine.

You may notice the abbreviation nm on the outer packaging of many of these tools. This stands for nanometers and refers to the wavelength of the light that the device emits—an important metric to consider, says dermatologist Jody A. Levine, MD. "Red light typically falls between 630 and 660 nanometers, and is good for targeting fine lines and mild discoloration," says Dr. Levine. If you're looking for something slightly more powerful—to deal with deeper wrinkles, sagging, or stubborn pigmentary problems—go with a device that cranks up to the near-infrared range (between 800 and 850 nanometers) to penetrate deeper.

Our beauty team is well-versed in red light therapy tools. We’ve been updating this story since December 2022—and I’ve been writing about these devices since November 2019. I've also been using red light therapy tools since April 2018. They've significantly diminished my stubborn fine lines and hyperpigmentation—and when I stop for a few months, they slowly reappear. Consistency is key, so we tested dozens of red light therapy devices for over two years to determine which ones are worth purchasing and can help us maintain wrinkle-free skin.

Since there are quite literally thousands of options available on Amazon alone, I asked dermatologists about their no-fail picks. Next, I recruited WH staffers—beauty director Brian Underwood, associate style & commerce editor Shannen Zitz, and associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian—and our beauty contributors—Erica Metzger, Lily Wohlner, and Lisa DeSantis—for their suggestions. After compiling a comprehensive list of promising new launches, old standbys, and products that align with derm guidance, we got to testing.

We spent a minimum of three weeks evaluating attributes like ease of use, treatment time, comfort, any tangible results, and overall value. Of the 22 devices tested, these 10 delivered the best results in our in-depth testing process.

Beyond keeping expert guidance in mind—type, nanometers, and time commitment—we considered our long- and short-term results. We also considered each product’s durability over the years, and eliminated anything that doesn’t remain in top shape. Ahem, don’t forget to clean your LED face masks to help with their longevity. We also tried the latest drops and the Women’s Health Beauty Award-winning Solawave Neck & Chest Pro Light Therapy Mask took the crown as our favorite launch of the year. Ultimately, these are the devices that we’ll continue to use and would genuinely repurchase if we had to start our skincare routine from scratch. The best part? Our faves start at just $72, which is a major win for a category that easily ranges from $300 to $700.

In-office LED lights operate at more powerful strengths than at-home devices, which increases efficacy. So, with professional treatments, you may see better results in less time, but that doesn't mean you should dismiss the at-home devices altogether. They're still helpful for treating common skin conditions like the odd breakout or fine lines, but it could take up to six months to start seeing results, says Dr. Sperling. Our experts also say they're a great way to maintain the results from any in-office treatments you may be receiving.

If you want to get faster and more effective results at home without a trip to your dermatologist's office or a medi-spa, Dr. Patel recommends using your device more often—if possible daily.

While many red light devices are generally safe, start out by using yours once or twice a week to make sure your skin doesn't have any reactions. Once you've confirmed that your skin can tolerate it, Dr. Sperling says you can increase the frequency, according to the brand’s instructions.You can use your red light therapy device in the morning or at night, but ideally, it should be done on clean, dry, product-free skin after you cleanse your face. However, Dr. Patel notes that if you use a red light therapy tool after a serum, it'll help the product penetrate more deeply into the skin—just patch test on some skin before you do it on the whole face.

It sounds obvious, but read the instructions carefully and don’t use the device on infected skin, says Dr. Patel. Most LED face masks come with goggles to shield your eyes; wearing them offers essential protection. And, be sure that you don't fall asleep with the mask or tool on your face longer than instructed or it can result in scars and burns, says Dr. Camp. Most tools have an auto turn-off feature, but if yours doesn’t, then set a timer on your smartphone.

#4850. Fall Weddings Are More Popular Than Ever. Here's How to Dress for One (The Right Way)

Autumn is now the most popular season to tie the knot.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WEDDINGS CAN be hard to dress for, and this isn’t limited to those directly involved; being a mere attendant requires some degree of planning. I’ve attended quite a few weddings over the last year, both as a groomsman and as a regular guest, both with their own sartorial challenges. (I actually found it more stressful not being in the wedding party, at least in one aspect: I had to pick out my own outfit. This also allowed for a little creativity.)

I covered some options for summer weddings a few months back, and just like that, we’re on to the next season. Fall has arguably become the season for weddings; in fact, October recently overtook June as the most popular month for weddings in the U.S. I can attest to this; I was in two separate ones last October.

Summer and fall weddings have quite a few differences. You can get away with some more “fun” looks in the summer, and you can get a little more creative with the materials (linen, seersucker, etc.). Fall weddings are typically a little more buttoned-up, but there’s a little wiggle room there, too.

I’ll go through some of the easiest ways for guys to dress for an autumn affair—with different wedding types in mind—to get you off the ground. We also included plenty of price points because, as everyone knows, weddings can get expensive fast.

Brooks Brothers Explorer Collection Non-Iron Twill Button Down Collar

Cole Haan Men's Grand Neoclassic Plain Toe Oxfords

We’ll start with what we consider a traditional wedding: a separate ceremony at a church, chapel, or the wedding venue without a black-tie dress code. This is about as classic as it gets, so you don’t have to go overboard—but we do recommend wearing a timeless suit. Our style team has tested plenty of affordable menswear brands offering solid options that approximate the look and fit of made-to-measure tailoring. One of them is the Black Tux, an upstart that offers suits for both rental and purchase, with virtual and in-person fittings to match you with the closest standard size. The prices are great, too: the Essential Suit is just under $300 all in. We also happened to score a 20 percent off code for the Black Tux, made exclusively for Men’s Health readers. Just use code MH20 at checkout (minimum of $295). The code’s good until October 31. Most of its higher-priced suits also include a rental option, but for the extra $100 or so, we’d recommend just buying one. The True Navy is a safe color you can wear year-round. The Grey Suit is a step up and is made from a heavier—but still breathable—merino wool. Perfect for the autumn temperatures.

A classic dress shirt is more than okay, but if you want to stand out in an otherwise pretty basic look, you can go with a classic twill dress shirt like this one from Brooks Brothers. You can get a little bit more creative with the tie, but nothing too crazy; the left-to-right diagonal stripes of a classic rep tie keep it distinguished. A Classic Textured Solid Tie is always a safe bet, too. Baby blue and pink go well with a gray suit, and navy, black, and red look better with gray. The shoes are easy, too: black plain-toe oxfords for grays, and these simple brown Astorflex Loafers with a crisp navy blue.

Brooks Brothers Classic Fit Double-Breasted Wool Pinstripe 1818 Suit

Charles Tyrwhitt Cotton Pocket Square - White

Mack Weldon Silver Extended Crew Dress Sock

The Black Tux Picture Frame Brushed Gold Tie Bar

Black-tie affairs probably require even less creativity, but there are definitely ways to push the envelope to stand out. The safe choice, of course, is the classic tux. If you plan to need one on multiple occasions, we also love that the Black Tux once again gets top marks; its Essential option is also under $300. There are some pricier options you can also rent, but the Essential Tux is low-key enough to rock at any formal occasion. SuitShop is another upstart offering ready-to-wear tuxedos at accessible prices, including several options under $300. Accessories-wise, you can opt for a super fancy pair of onyx cufflinks from one of our favorite watch brands, Shinola, but something a little more budget-friendly is more than okay.

Nowadays, you don’t have to go all-black, at least depending on the event. But if you do deviate, you'd better make it count. Like upgrading to a double-breasted suit, for example. The Classic Fit Double-Breasted Wool Pinstripe 1818 Suit elevates your look without making you look like a Prohibition-era mobster (surprisingly, a very fine line).

The other big component of all of this: your shoes. You probably don’t want to go with a loafer; an oxford or derby shoe is the better option. Our favorite: Cole Haan’s Hawthorne Oxfords, a classic dress shoe that’s made with the brand’s famously comfortable insoles so your dogs will stay happy for hours. It’s also versatile enough to wear at dressy events or in a more casual office vibe. In other words, you’ll be getting a lot of use out of it.

If you want to go all out, you can go full custom. Go big or go home, as they say. If you’re in the NYC area, Alan David Custom is a great choice. The bespoke tailor will give you a sample suit to try on before making final decisions, and the experience is a throwback to classier times. They’ll even ship it to you when it’s all said and done. If you want to go fully custom, you’ll also need the shoes to match.

Bonobos Empire Stretch Italian Wool Tuxedo

Todd Snyder Italian Lightweight Sutton Jacket

Quince Supima Cotton Herringbone Dress Shirt

Todd Snyder Relaxed Fit Japanese Selvedge Chino

Reigning Champ Stretch Chino Marina Standard Pant

Allen Edmonds Rhett Cap-toe Oxford Dress Shoe

Cocktail weddings give you a little more freedom than a traditional one. Here, you can rock a classic suit or a nice blazer and slacks, and you wouldn’t be wrong either way. The classic Ludlow tux from J.Crew gives off serious old-school cocktail jacket vibes, and it’s reserved for swankier occasions. Todd Snyder’s Italian Lightweight Sutton Jacket is another high-end option that’s both breathable and easy to wear throughout the night. If you wear blazers regularly, you’ll also get plenty of use out of this, even into the hotter months. Todd Snyder also makes our favorite pair of relaxed-fit chinos that check a lot of boxes for us. The Relaxed Fit Japanese Selvedge Chino is a steep departure from the ones we wear to the office, which is why it’s such a legit option for dressier occasions.

If the baggier fit (and higher price tag) is scaring you off a bit, Reigning Champ makes an ultra-breathable cotton-twill chino that wears more like a standard dress pant. They’re comfortable, breathable, and have a little added stretch; you’ll get a lot of use out of them outside the wedding. The other big component of all of this: your shoes. You probably don’t want to go with a loafer; an Oxford or derby shoe is the better option. Our style team loves Allen Edmonds’. It’s made with calfskin leather, with a surprisingly light-yet-cushioned outsole that’s comfortable enough to use all night.

Billy Reid Exploded Glen Plaid Archie Jacket

Brooks Brothers Straight-Fit Cotton Advantage Chino Pants

Brooks Brothers Friday Shirt, Oxford Patterns

Madewell Johnny-Collar Sweater Polo in Slub Knit Cotton

Cole Haan Zerogrand Remastered Wing Tip Oxford

Barns have since had a huge come-up and are now a hugely popular wedding venue. Regardless of your stance on barn weddings, you have to dress a little differently. Vineyard weddings (and really any outdoor event) live in that same category. If you’re looking at a late-fall event, you’ll want something a little warmer. The Grey Plaid Wool Suit is a step up in that department without being too overbearing; the subtle designs also scream fall. You can also go with the blazer-and-dress-pants route. Abercrombie’s A&F Collins Blazer is a fantastic budget option, and the Olive Stripe colorway similarly gives off fall vibes. It’s easy to pair with dressier chinos, like the Straight-Fit Cotton Advantage Chino Pants from Brooks Brothers. They’re essentially dress pants with a certain chinoesque comfort.

If you do go this route, you can have a little fun with the undershirt; Brooks Brothers’ Friday Shirt can add some flair to your getup. Madewell’s Johnny-Collar Sweater Polo is also a nice departure from your traditional button-down (and a lot more comfortable, too). If the wedding isn’t all that fancy, you can get away with rocking some of the most comfortable dress shoes/sneakers out there: Cole Haan’s Zerogrand Remastered Wing Tip Oxfords.

Buck Mason Capitola Linen Carry-On Jacket

Bonobos Stretch Weekday Warrior Dress Pants

Reigning Champ Heavyweight Jersey OG T-Shirt

The destination wedding can definitely be a challenge, depending on how close you are to the person (or people) getting married. They’re always a great time, though, and you can get similarly creative. We suggest a travel blazer; you’re already shelling out a lot of money for flights and accommodations, so you can save a few bucks by not checking a full suit. Our style director, Christian Gollayan, recently did a full review of the Bonobos Jetsetter Knit Blazer. He described it as a “lifesaver” when traveling. You can definitely rock it at a fall destination wedding, especially considering the hardworking knit construction. For a lighter, beachy vibe, Buck Mason’s Capitola Linen Carry-On Jacket is my own go-to. It holds its shape well for linen, and some of the darker colors work well for any season.

Pants are easy to pack, so we’d suggest going with something that helps you stand out. #4848. Wellness Apps, Medically Tailored Meals Help Slow Weight Gain After GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Weight regain is common after stopping GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

In fact, previous research has shown that most people regain at least half of their lost weight within 1 year of stopping treatment, with weight regain often accelerating during the first 3–4 months.

However, a new study suggests that structured support, including a weight management app or medically tailored meals, may help slow weight regain after discontinuing GLP-1 medications.

The small study, published October 7 in Obesity Science & Practice, found that participants who received either intervention regained significantly less weight over four months than those receiving usual care.

The study included 39 adults with an average age of 50, an average weight of 189 pounds, and an average body mass index (BMI) of 31.4.

All participants had lost more than 10% of their body weight while taking GLP-1 medications and had stopped treatment within the previous 30 days.

All participants also completed questionnaires at the beginning and end of the study and used Bluetooth scales to track their weight at home throughout the four-month period.

Researchers randomly assigned participants to one of the following three groups:

Participants continued to receive care from their healthcare providers, which may include nutrition, exercise, and lifestyle counseling from a clinician or registered dietitian. The type and amount of support varied depending on the provider’s recommendations and available resources. The researchers did not provide any additional intervention.

Participants received a subscription to Noom, an app that uses behavioral strategies to support weight loss and maintenance. These include tracking food intake, exercise, and weight, as well as educational lessons on the psychological, physiological, social, and environmental factors that influence eating behaviors.

The app also provides tools to help users recognize and manage triggers that may lead to overeating. Participants were encouraged to use the app for at least 15 minutes daily, including completing lessons, logging food, and tracking their weight.

These are typically nutrient-dense meals developed by registered dietitians to meet the nutritional needs of people with specific health conditions, such as chronic kidney disease or uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

For this study, participants in this group selected 10 portion-controlled, “weight wellness” meals each week from more than 70 options, which were delivered to their homes.

After four months, participants who received either medically tailored meals or access to the digital weight management app experienced significantly less weight regain than those receiving usual care.

The estimated weight regain was 10.75% of body weight in the usual-care group, compared with 3.6% in the Noom group and 3.58% in the medically tailored meals group.

Although participants in all three groups regained weight, the findings suggest that structured nutritional or behavioral support may help limit weight regain after stopping GLP-1 medications.

“These findings highlight the benefits of ongoing support for patients on a weight loss journey,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA. Ali wasn’t involved in the study.

Denise Pate, MD, a board certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan who was also not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are significant “because they show that obesity management is multifactorial, not only medication, but the combination of types of meals and behavioral change all play a role.”

However, because this was a small, four-month study, larger, longer-term trials are needed to determine whether these approaches can help people maintain weight loss over time after stopping GLP-1 medications.

Ali noted that research suggests GLP-1 medications are most effective for weight management when taken long-term.

“Obesity needs to be recognized and treated as a chronic condition, similar to diabetes or hypertension,” he said.

Pate agreed, emphasizing that obesity is not always recognized as a chronic condition that may require ongoing treatment.

“I feel that the medical community, insurance, and the population as a whole have yet to fully accept obesity as a chronic medical condition, which it most definitely is for a large part of patients. For this reason, I think patients should stay on these medications long term if needed,” she said.

“GLP-1 medications are highly effective tools for transitioning to a healthier diet and lifestyle, which for most people may require long-term use,” Ali added.

Pate explained that one of the goals of GLP-1 medications is to help people eat smaller portions by recognizing when they feel full and stopping when they do.

“I tell my patients from the start, this is the goal,” she said, adding that she hopes patients will retain those habits after stopping treatment.

Ali recommended maintaining a balanced diet rich in protein and vegetables while limiting added sugars and refined carbohydrates.

He added that tracking apps and regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian may also help people maintain their progress.

“Patients need to understand that the GLP medication is not a miracle drug, although with the dramatic weight loss, it can be perceived as such. It is only a tool to be used in conjunction with an exercise routine as well as a healthy diet,” Pate said.

#4847. Is Pilates Effective For Weight Loss? Instructors Share How To Incorporate It Into Your Routine

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It’s nearly impossible to scroll through social media right now without seeing some celebrity or influencer rave about the perks of Pilates. But even with all the buzz surrounding this popular practice, details are a little fuzzy on whether Pilates is an effective workout for weight loss.

First off, know that the health and fitness benefits of having a Pilates practice are so much more than that. This form of exercise is known for improving your posture, breathing, flexibility, and core strength. As Claudette Sariya, CPT, a personal trainer and fitness educator based in New York City, notes, “any movement that you can enjoy regularly and consistently can help you lose weight.”

So, doing Pilates (or any workout for that matter) to stay active paired with a nutrition plan is likely to help you with weight loss. But it probably won't help expedite your weight loss in the same way that, say, lifting heavy weights would. (We'll get into why!)

The focus of Pilates is not weight loss, experts point out. "Pilates should be considered part of your self-care routine," says Jacquelyn Brennan, CSCS, pilates instructor and co-founder of Chicago-based Pilates and Coffee. "We all need to move our spines more, move our joints through every range of motion, and everyone needs to be breathing better."

All of those healthy practices together can aid weight loss, though. Here's everything to know about doing Pilates when you're trying to lose weight.

Meet the experts: Gabbi Berkow, RD, CPT, is a nutritionist and Pilates instructor. Jacquelyn Brennan, CSCS, is a Pilates instructor and co-founder of Chicago-based Pilates and Coffee. Claudette Sariya, CPT, is a personal trainer and fitness educator based in New York City. Sonja R. Price Herbert is a certified Pilates instructor and founder of Black Girl Pilates. Nofar Hagag is a Pilates instructor and creator of the Nofar Method.

One form of Pilates isn't superior to another to drop pounds, experts agree. "For weight loss, I don’t think one type of Pilates is necessarily best,” says Berkow. Yet, there are different flavors—and finding one that you enjoy and will keep coming back to can, in turn, help you commit to a fitness routine and lose weight.

When someone mentions Pilates, they're often referring to Romana’s Pilates, which features exercises that Joseph Pilates (the founder) developed, explains Gabbi Berkow, RD, CPT, a nutritionist and Pilates instructor. Some studios are dedicated to classical or Romana’s Pilates (which is what Berkow is trained in) but there are studios that feature different Pilates-based workouts, which means they use Pilates-inspired moves but don't follow the classical version to a T. Some Pilates classes take place on a mat (a.k.a. mat Pilates), while others occur on a reformer, which is basically a sliding, spring-loaded platform.

You also might hear the term "athletic Pilates," but that is usually a description of the pace, says Sonja R. Price Herbert, a certified Pilates instructor and founder of Black Girl Pilates. These classes are designed to be fast-paced and high-intensity, and may even have some high-intensity interval training (HIIT) exercises and elements in the mix, which would make them better for weight loss due to the way HIIT training can help you burn more calories during and after the workout.

But if you really want to maximize your Pilates practice for weight loss and strength, it’s a good idea to use both the reformer and Cadillac machines, says Nofar Hagag, a Pilates instructor and creator of the Nofar Method. “By incorporating cardio-focused movements—such as squats, planks, and Pilates burpees, your heart rate increases, boosting calorie burn and metabolism,” she says. “These high-energy moves are paired with strength-training exercises, like side leg lifts and abs teasers, to build lean muscle and improve body composition.” (Reminder: Loading your muscles with resistance is key for muscle growth—and more muscle mass helps you burn more calories at rest and, in turn, lose weight.)

What you also want when it comes to Pilates and weight loss: an instructor who knows what they’re doing, is committed to safe movements, and who will challenge you, says Berkow. “You want to make sure your Pilates class is a workout. It shouldn’t be just a series of slow, easy stretches. Pilates has to contribute to your total daily calorie burn for it to make a difference in weight loss,” she says.

If you’ve ever gone to a class, you know how insane the core work is (seriously, the famed Hundreds exercise is not for the faint of heart...or abs).

While you cannot spot-reduce fat, Pilates can help you learn how to properly engage your pelvic floor and deep core muscles, says Brennan. "Pilates will teach you how to engage your muscles correctly, which will lend to increased activation during core exercises and lead to [the appearance of a] 'tighter tummy,' " she says.

However, to see abs definition, you do have to lose the fat that sits on top of your muscles, which requires proper nutrition, says Berkow. Think: a diet rich in whole, fresh foods and a limit on overly-processed foods and snacks.

There is some research to suggest that you can lose weight doing Pilates—but it's tough to give an exact number of pounds considering so many individual factors play into weight loss, such as genetics, sleep and stress, lifestyle habits, and more.

A meta-analysis of 11 randomized controlled trials published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2021 found that pilates “dramatically” reduced body weight and body fat percentage in adults with overweight or obesity. And the longer the person practiced Pilates, the bigger the weight loss. Older research has had mixed results, though, with one small study concluding Pilates was indeed helpful for weight loss, while another found it had no impact on weight loss in post-menopausal women.

You want a mat that offers a little extra cushion than the standard yoga mat to protect your vertebrae when rolling onto your back.

ProBody Pilates Ring And Mini Exercise Ball

Pilates teachers love a good prop. You may want to have a few options—like this Pilates ring (a.k.a. magic circle) and ball set—handy for online classes.

Many studios require sticky socks for both safety and sanitary reasons, so stashing a pair in your gym bag is always a good idea. These Pointe Studio socks offer a non-slip bottom in tons of cute colors and patterns.

Looking for a mat that's a bit more aesthetic? The 8mm-sized Bala Play Mat is another cushy option (and it’s antimicrobial, to boot!).

If you want to invest in your Pilates practice, this home reformer is a cult favorite that often shows up in professional studios. During testing, we found this machine to have a sleek, low profile, sturdy frame, and impressive footbar adjustability.

Again, traditional Pilates isn’t a modality designed for weight loss. Generally, traditional classes do not pack enough of a cardio or strength training component, Herbert says: “It is not a steady-state [cardio modality] like running, jumping, or walking. There is also not enough weight [or resistance] to aid in a decrease in body fat.” Instead, Herbert says that “Pilates focuses on awareness of the body, efficiency of movement, and breath.”

Pilates will, however, deliver far more benefits than just a lower number on a scale that may indirectly help with weight loss. For instance, Pilates involves breath work, encouraging deeper belly breaths that are in direct contrast to the shallow breathing many of us do on the regular. “Shallow breathing leads to increased cortisol levels, which contributes to weight gain. One could say that through pilates and learning to breathe better, you’d have lower cortisol—and thus, stress—levels, something that can help you lose weight,” Brennan says.

Feeling better, both mentally and physically, will also encourage you to take care of your body, says Berkow—and Pilates can definitely be a key part of achieving an overall weight-loss goal.

#4845. Honda has dominated motorcycles for decades. Electric bikes are changing that

Honda has spent decades building one of the most dominant positions in the global motorcycle industry, selling millions of gasoline-powered two-wheelers each year. But in markets where electric motorcycles and scooters are becoming increasingly accessible, that dominance is starting to face a serious challenge.

Vietnam offers a particularly interesting case study, where rapidly growing electric motorcycle sales are beginning to reshape a market long dominated by Honda.

According to newly released nationwide sales figures, Vietnam saw more than 3 million motorcycle and scooter sales during the first nine months of 2026, representing 25.9% growth over the same period last year.

But the real story is in the electric segment, where sales surged 90.5% to reach 973,247 units. That means electric two-wheelers now account for approximately 32% of all new motorcycle and scooter sales in the country.

And the biggest beneficiary isn’t Honda. It’s actually Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast.

While Honda remains Vietnam’s largest motorcycle manufacturer overall, with sales growing 8.4% this year, VinFast has surged into second place with a staggering 152.1% increase in sales. Yamaha now sits in third place, followed by electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea in fourth.

Of the top four players, half are electric, and it’s precisely that half that is experiencing meteoric sales growth.

It’s an impressive reshuffling of a market that has traditionally been dominated by Japanese gasoline motorcycle manufacturers.

Vietnam’s transition hasn’t happened in a vacuum, either. Government efforts to reduce urban air pollution, including plans to restrict gasoline-powered motorcycles in parts of Hanoi, have helped create an increasingly favorable environment for electric alternatives.

Too bad for Honda but I'm thrilled to read about increasing sales of electric motorcycles. I don't live in or near Vietnam but the pollution from small gasoline engines affects everyone where the wind blows it.

And with companies like VinFast offering an expanding range of electric scooters and motorcycles, riders now have more practical alternatives to gasoline-powered models than ever before.

To be clear, Honda isn’t exactly struggling. Its motorcycle sales are still growing, and the Japanese giant remains the undisputed market leader in Vietnam. But its overall share of the market is shrinking, and its relatively modest growth compared to the exploding electric segment suggests that the market’s center of gravity is beginning to shift.

Vietnam may be just a single example, but it’s an important one of what can happen when electric two-wheelers become viable mainstream alternatives to gasoline motorcycles.

Honda has spent decades perfecting the gasoline motorcycle. The question now is how quickly it can adapt to a market that is increasingly interested in something else.

#4844. I imported a $2,000 electric truck from China. Five years later, here’s the truth

Five years ago, I did something that seemed pretty ridiculous at the time. I bought a $2,000 electric mini-truck from China, had it shipped across the oceans to the US, and put it to work on my parents’ property in Florida.

The little white mini electric truck became something of an internet sensation, with my original unboxing and testing video quickly racking up over 10 million views, plus several million more from the follow-up videos.

It also attracted plenty of skeptics who were convinced that a $2,000 Chinese electric truck would fall apart within months, rust into oblivion, or otherwise prove to be a spectacular waste of money. “Good thing it has a bed,” was a common refrain. “So you can collect all the pieces that fall off along the way.”

I gave an update after the first year, showing that the truck was doing great. But to be fair, one year doesn’t tell us much.

Well now it’s been over five years, and I recently returned to Florida to see how the little truck has held up after five trips around the sun on my parents’ homestead. And I’ve got to say, the results are pretty surprising.

So here’s the truth about how the truck is doing five years later. Oh, and if you want to see it in action, you can check out my update video here. Trust me, you’ll want to.

First, it’s important to understand that this truck hasn’t spent five years sitting in a garage as some kind of novelty vehicle. It’s been a genuine workhorse on my parents’ 10-acre homestead.

Over the years, we’ve used it to haul everything from mulch and sand to lumber, tree branches, logs, yard waste, and everything in between.

Its hydraulic dump bed makes it particularly useful for moving bulk materials around the property, like hauling mulch and then dumping it in their raised planting beds.

My dad even uses it as a mobile irrigation truck during Florida’s dry season. I built him a solar-powered pump system that fills a water bladder in the truck’s bed with water from his pond, allowing him to drive around watering his trees and plants.

By now, it’s been involved in practically every major landscaping and construction project my parents have tackled.

We’ve also made some improvements over the years. Early on, my dad and I replaced the ridiculously stiff factory suspension springs with softer ones, making the ride considerably more comfortable. We added a custom tow hitch and swapped the original street tires for aggressive off-road tires that work much better on the property’s sandy and muddy terrain.

The suspension upgrade did reduce how much weight we can comfortably carry, though. Load more than around 500 pounds (220 kg) of sand or other bulk materials into the bed, and the rear end starts squatting enough that our homemade tow hitch threatens to touch grass.

But for most of the work we do, it’s been an excellent little utility vehicle.

And before anyone asks, no, this isn’t a street-legal truck. It was never really designed for American roads, and we use it almost exclusively on private property. Sure, it’s hit the pavement a few times since they live out in the boonies and its normal to see tractors and other non-street-legal vehicles on country roads, but it’s not the most ideal vehicle for long distance transport at 25 mph (40 km/h).

Here’s the part that surprised me most: Almost everything still works.

The electric windows still zip up and down with the speed of a guillotine. The electric door locks work. The headlights work. The backup camera works. Even the air conditioning still blows impressively cold air.

I actually checked that last one with a thermal camera during my latest visit, and the air coming out of the vents was around 55°F (12°C). Not bad for a five-year-old air conditioning system in a $2,000 truck!

The windshield wiper still operates, but its range of motion has decreased significantly. It now stops around the middle of the driver’s field of vision, which isn’t ideal when Florida’s famous afternoon thunderstorms roll through.

The rearview mirror has also developed an annoying habit of falling off. We’ve glued it back on multiple times, and it looks like another round of adhesive surgery is coming soon.

Inside, there’s some minor upholstery damage on the driver’s seat, including a few small tears and stressed seams in the cheap faux-leather material that you can see in the video.

The passenger seat, which sees much less use, still looks nearly new. In another few years, I might just swap the two seats to get another half decade or so out of them before we need some upholstery repair.

One decorative plastic panel around the driver’s door handle has popped off, though I still have the piece and could probably snap it back into place with a bit of effort. It’s just aesthetic though, so it’s been a low-priority repair.

And that’s pretty much the extent of the mechanical and electrical problems we’ve encountered.

There haven’t been any major drivetrain failures, the hydraulic dump bed still works, and the truck continues to start up and drive just as reliably as it did when it was new.

It still gets used for lots of bulk jobs, material hauling, and sometimes just random transportation around the property.

One of the biggest predictions from critics five years ago was that this cheap Chinese truck would quickly dissolve into a pile of rust.

To be fair, there is some rust. But nowhere near as much as you might expect.

Most of the corrosion is concentrated in areas where the paint has been scratched or chipped, especially around the tailgate and cargo bed.

The rustiest spot is definitely the top lip of the tailgate, where we usually have long objects hanging out of the bed, such as shovels, ladders, lumber, etc. The paint has worn through on that edge, and the rust has inevitably started in those few spots.

The truck is stored outdoors under a lean-to roof that I built between two shipping containers, but we have a skid-steer in front of it and so the rear of the truck sticks out and gets rained on several times a week (or several times a day during the summer).

We applied a paint-on bed liner during the truck’s first year, which helped protect the metal for quite a while.

After four years of hauling dirt, rocks, branches, and other abrasive materials though, that coating has started wearing through in a few places.

Every time I’m shoveling mulch out of the bed and I hear that scrape of metal on metal, I cringe just a bit before remembering that the truck cost me $2,000 and doesn’t owe me anything at this point.

Speaking of being parked outdoors with the rear hanging out for the world (and the UV) to see, there’s clearly an effect on the truck’s wear.

You can absolutely see the difference in the paint and plastic components. The front headlight lenses are still crystal clear, while the rear taillight lenses have become noticeably cloudy from UV exposure.

Despite that, the truck’s basic structure remains solid, and the rust is mostly cosmetic and limited to the high-impact areas that tend to get beaten up repeatedly, as you’d expect in any self-respecting work truck.

Considering that Florida combines high humidity, frequent rain, and intense sunshine, I’d call that a pretty impressive result for a vehicle that cost less than many electric bicycles.

Since the truck lives at my parents’ property, my dad has actually spent far more time using it than I have.

And when I asked him how he felt about the purchase after five years, he was surprisingly enthusiastic.

He described the truck as an incredibly functional piece of equipment that has become an essential part of maintaining the property.

In fact, he pointed out that the truck has been involved in virtually every significant project they’ve completed over the past five years.

It isn’t the only electric utility vehicle on the property anymore. My parents also have a Kandi electric UTV, which has taken over some of the smaller daily chores thanks to its better suspension and more convenient dump bed operation (the bed also lowers under power) which helps my dad lift the trash and recycling bins and drive them down the long private road to the street on pickup day.

But when it’s time to haul bulky loads, long branches, or large quantities of dirt and mulch, the Changli is still the vehicle of choice.

My dad also pointed out something that tends to get lost in discussions about cheap Chinese EVs: the operating costs have been almost nonexistent.

A full charge costs a little over a dollar in electricity, and the truck has required remarkably little maintenance over the years.

Even after five years, he says it still puts a smile on his face every time he drives it.

Yes, the truck cost me $2,000. Or technically, the price was $2,080.00, and that’s what I paid to the factory. At that point, it was mine.

Of course, it was still in China though, and so I had to pay an international freight company to have it sent on a cargo ship to the US (nearly $2,000 by itself, if I recall correctly).

Then I had to pay the US Treasury a bunch of tariffs to help make sure American automotive companies don’t have to compete with these types of vehicles.

And I also had to hire a customs broker to handle the import documentation for me, etc.

So there were several thousand dollars of additional fees on top of it, but I still think it was worth it based on the incredible amount of use it has given us over the years.

Of course, there’s an important caveat here for anyone considering getting a vehicle like this.

Remember, this is a very basic, low-speed electric utility vehicle without the safety equipment, crash protection, or regulatory approvals you’d expect from a modern full-size pickup truck.

It’s not something I’d recommend as a replacement for a road-going vehicle.

This is a work truck for us. It moves material, tows trailers and boats, carries the trash cans a quarter mile to the street each week, etc. In that way, as a private-property work truck, it’s been fantastic.

But even though I’m calling it simple, that doesn’t mean it wasn’t made pretty well. The truck has hauled countless loads, survived five years of rough Florida weather, and required very little maintenance. Even its cheap interior and basic electronics have held up better than I expected.

I also have to give some credit to the modifications we made early on, especially the suspension and tire upgrades, which turned a quirky little imported vehicle into something much more practical for off-road work.

The biggest unknown is how much longer it will last. Unfortunately, the truck doesn’t have a proper odometer, so I can’t even tell you how many miles we’ve accumulated over five years of driving around the property.

I also can’t tell you anything about battery degradation, since we don’t know how far it has driven (due to the lack of odometer), and the fact that even on 10 acres, you just can’t get that far from an outlet. We generally charge the 6 kWh battery every couple weeks just to keep it topped up, but range was never an issue and hasn’t become one, at least not for our use case. If you needed to drive this thing to the next town over each day, it could be another story.

Nothing like being forced to drive massive four-door trucks that weigh as much as four cars because your country is protecting monopolist manufacturers and only allows their land yachts for sale.

Basically, there’s no indication that the mini-truck is nearing the end of its useful life.

My dad thinks it could easily serve another five or even ten years, and after seeing how well it’s survived its first five, I’m inclined to agree that there’s plenty of life left in it.

When I first bought this thing, plenty of people told me it was a terrible idea. Five years later, with the truck still hauling dirt, carrying branches, and generally earning its keep, I’m feeling pretty good about that decision. It’s done a lot more in its five years than many “real” pickup trucks do in their entire lives.

Not bad for a funny little electric truck from China.

LED face masks are hands-free, so you can wear one while on your phone, reading, or watching TV. Here’s what to know when purchasing the best LED face mask.

Most at-home red light therapy devices use a mix of red and blue wavelengths. However, each LED shade offers different benefits, so you’ll need to find the right color for the skin concerns you want to treat, says dermatologist Leah Ansell, MD. Here’s a quick guide:

Standardized wavelengths are helpful, but the number of lights is also important, says dermatologist Azadeh Shirazi, MD. A higher concentration of LED bulbs provides more even coverage.

Not all LED face masks are built the same.

Carving out time for self-care in your busy schedule can sometimes feel like a stretch. Thankfully, these LED face masks require a relatively low time commitment. With such speedy treatment, it’s no wonder the makeup artists for Halle Berry and Carey Mulligan have primped their clients using CurrentBody Skin.

LED face masks are usually class II devices. They’re either FDA-listed or FDA-registered, meaning the brand notified the agency about the device. However, this listing doesn’t indicate the products are approved, cleared, or authorized by the agency.

They could also be FDA-cleared, meaning they are similar to other devices that are legally marketed for the same use. Our editors prioritized testing face masks that are either FDA-listed, -registered, or -cleared. And I referenced the FDA database to verify the status of our recommendations.

If you're fidgety and can't commit to sitting still or lying down for 15 minutes straight, look for a cordless option. Now if comfort is king, look for adjustable straps, a padded interior, or a flexible outer shell. TheraFace boasts all of these features and even vibrates for extra relaxation.

Yes, it’s generally low-risk for most users, says dermatologist Dendy Engelman, MD. "LED light therapy is not an invasive treatment, and when done properly, the risks are minimal," she says. A 2018 study in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology points out that this treatment has an "excellent" safety profile, Dr. Ansell says. While they're safe to use on the skin, there's concern about eye damage from these lights. So, it's a good idea to wear the eye inserts to help protect them.

If you’re photosensitive or have connective tissue conditions, you should either skip LED light therapy or approach it with caution, advises Dr. Ansell. If neither issue is a problem for you, Dr. Engelman suggests wearing it a few times a week, but it's crucial to refer to your specific mask's instructions for the recommended time.

Start with clean skin, says Dr. Engelman. After washing your face in the morning or at night, set your mask to the proper wavelength, then put on goggles. Comfort is key, so feel free to adjust any straps and align yourself with the cushioning (if your mask has any) before using it. Post-use, finish the rest of your skincare routine, and definitely use it before applying retinol, says Dr. Shirazi.

#4842. Fitbit Edge vs. Fitbit Air: Which New Fitbit Should You Buy?

Do you want a less distracting tracker or one with a screen and built-in GPS?

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

GOOGLE DIDN’T RELEASE a major new Fitbit fitness tracker for two and a half years after the Charge 6 came out in October 2023. Then it released two new models in five months. The first, the $99 Fitbit Air, came out in May and works a lot like a Whoop. You wear it day and night, and it sends your heart rate, sleep, and workout data to the Google Health app on your phone.Second is the $179 Fitbit Edge, which followed in October as the Charge 6’s successor. It offers the same features as the Air and adds a 1.34-inch screen, built-in GPS, and an ECG app that checks your heart rhythm for signs of atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that raises your stroke risk. Both trackers pair with iPhones and Android phones, so neither is exclusive to Google’s platform.For most people, deciding between them comes down to one question: do you want to see your pace and heart rate on your wrist during a workout, or are you fine checking everything on your phone afterward?

With no screen and no buttons, the Fitbit Air is as simple as they come to use. Google rates its battery at up to seven days, so you won’t have to charge every night. It’s also the cheaper way to get Google’s Health Coach. The $99 price includes three free months of Google’s Health Premium, which costs $9.99 a month after that.The Fitbit Edge shows your pace and heart rate on its screen during a workout, and its built-in GPS records your route without your phone. If you run or ride outdoors, you can leave your phone at home and still come back with a map and split times. The Edge also has two sensors the Air doesn’t: electrical sensors for the ECG app, and an altimeter that measures elevation gain on a hike and counts the floors you climb. It costs $80 more than the Air, and turning on its always-on display cuts the battery from about seven days to about two.

The Air’s tracker module is a 1.37 x 0.66-inch pod, and it’s about 25 percent smaller than the discontinued Fitbit Luxe. The pod pops out of its band and snaps into another one in a few seconds, so you can wear the fabric Performance Loop to sleep and switch to the silicone Active Band for a sweaty workout. If you want something dressier, the polyurethane Elevated Modern Band and a new Metal Mesh band are also available.The Edge measures 1.54 x 1.01 inches and is almost half an inch thick, with a pill-shaped body that’s noticeably larger than the Air. A side button opens the app list and takes you back to the clock face. It comes in Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon, with six band styles that run from the sweat-resistant Active Sport Band to a Metal Links bracelet. Both trackers are rated IP68 and 5ATM, which means they have dust and water protection.

The Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge record the same health data. Both measure your heart rate around the clock, plus blood oxygen, overnight skin temperature changes, and heart rate variability (HRV), the variation in time between heartbeats. HRV usually drops when you’re stressed, sick, or haven’t recovered from hard training.The Google Health app uses those readings to set a Readiness score each morning. It also tracks Cardio Load, which estimates how much cardiovascular strain your workouts create, while your personalized weekly target helps you balance activity and recovery. It can help you spot changes in your training load, but it can’t tell you exactly what your body can handle. Both trackers can alert you to an irregular rhythm that could be atrial fibrillation. They can also notify you when your heart rate stays unusually high or low while you’re inactive. Both also have Smart Wake, which vibrates to wake you during light sleep inside a time window you set.The Edge adds a few health tools the Air doesn’t have. Its ECG app records your heart’s electrical activity whenever you start a reading. If your heart feels like it’s racing or skipping, you can take a reading in the moment and save it to show your doctor. The Edge has a dedicated skin-temperature sensor, while older Fitbits such as the Charge 6 use a device-temperature sensor to track overnight skin-temperature variation.With Google Health Premium, both trackers get Google’s advanced Health Guardian features, which track trends in your blood pressure and insulin resistance. Google says they aren’t meant to screen or diagnose any condition.Both trackers start logging common workouts on their own. In my testing, the Air logged walks and lifting sessions without my starting them. Google says an update expands automatic detection on both the Air and Edge from 10 workout types to more than 100, including strength training, swimming, and racket sports. A workout only gets logged automatically if it lasts at least 15 minutes and keeps your heart rate up, so you may have to log short or stop-and-start sessions yourself.

The Fitbit Edge has built-in GPS, so it can map your route and measure your pace and distance without your phone. Google says the Edge’s GPS is up to 40 percent more accurate than its earlier trackers, thanks to a new GPS chip and case design. The Edge also has an altimeter, which reads air pressure to measure how much elevation you gain on a hilly run or how many floors you climb on a stair workout.The Edge’s screen also shows your stats during a workout, giving you instant feedback. You can set a pace target before a run and check on the screen whether you’re ahead of pace or lagging behind. During HIIT intervals, you can see which heart rate zone you’re in. On the track, it shows your split for each lap.The Fitbit Air has no GPS and no screen. To map a run, you have to carry your phone, and you can’t check your pace or heart rate until you look at the Google Health app afterward. If you mostly lift or walk and don’t want instant feedback, the Air is a great option. But if you care about your splits, the Edge is the better tracker.

The Fitbit Edge comes with nine apps, including Google Maps, Weather, and Timer. You can’t download more, and unlike the Pixel Watch 5, it doesn’t let you talk to Gemini from your wrist. Google Maps shows turn-by-turn directions on the Edge only after you start navigation on your phone, so you can’t look up a destination on the tracker itself.Calls and texts from your phone show up on the Edge’s screen. On Android, you can answer a text with a preset reply like “on my way.” Those quick replies don’t work with an iPhone, so iPhone owners can read texts on the Edge but have to answer them on the phone. Swiping down on the Edge opens a control panel where you can turn on Do Not Disturb, use the screen as a flashlight, or make your phone ring when you can’t find it.The Fitbit Air has none of this. Its only feature you’ll notice day to day is the Smart Wake alarm, which vibrates to wake you up. Everything else, including the Health Coach, lives in the Google Health app, which also syncs with Apple Health if you want your data in one place on an iPhone.Neither tracker has NFC, so you can’t use either one to pay with Google Wallet.

You don’t need a subscription to use either tracker. Without one, the Google Health app still shows your steps, heart rate, HRV, blood oxygen, sleep score and stages, Readiness, Cardio Load, and workouts. It also alerts you to an irregular heart rhythm. Google Health Premium costs $9.99 a month, and the Air and Edge each come with three months free.Premium adds the Gemini-powered Health Coach, which you can message anytime with questions about your data, plus weekly workout plans that adjust to your schedule. When I told it my shoulder was sore, it reworked that week’s plan around it. It also adds more detailed sleep summaries, meal logging from a photo, and plain-language summaries of your lab results.

The Charge 6 came out in 2023 and retails for $159.95. It has an ECG app and built-in GPS, and it can track more than 40 types of exercise. The Fitbit Edge improves on almost all of that. Its screen is 46 percent bigger, it’s rated IP68 for dust resistance, and it charges in about 90 minutes instead of two hours. And when the Edge’s battery wears out, you can replace it yourself instead of buying a new tracker.The Edge does drop two features the Charge 6 offers. The first is NFC, the chip that lets you pay with Google Wallet. The second is the EDA Scan app, which measures small changes in the sweat on your skin to estimate your stress level. If you’re buying a new tracker, the Charge 6 makes sense only if you pay with your wrist or find it well below the Edge’s $179 price (it’s down to $129.95 on Google’s site at the time of publication).The Fitbit Inspire 3 is the cheapest Fitbit with a screen, at about $100. It’s smaller than the Charge 6, lasts longer between charges, and starts tracking walks and runs automatically. It has no GPS or ECG, but it remains a solid choice if you want to see the time and your step count on your wrist without paying for the Edge.

Buy the Fitbit Air if you lift, walk, or take classes and mostly want to know how well you slept and how hard to train each day. At $99, it gets you the same heart rate, HRV, and sleep data as the Edge, and the same Health Coach if you pay for Premium. Because it has no screen, nothing on your wrist lights up or buzzes during dinner or in the middle of the night.For $80 more than the Air, the Edge gets you built-in GPS that maps your route and measures your pace without your phone. The screen shows your splits and heart rate zones while you’re moving, and the altimeter counts the elevation you climb. The ECG app also lets you check your heart rhythm the moment something feels off.If you already have a Charge 6, you don’t have to upgrade to get Google’s newest software. The Health Coach and Premium features come through the Google Health app, so they work on the tracker you already own. Upgrade to the Edge if the Charge 6’s battery no longer gets you through the week. But it’s worth keeping if you pay with your wrist. Neither new Fitbit has NFC, so the Charge 6 is the only one of the three that works with Google Wallet.
